docs.title: 1. What is Surge?
docs.text:
Surge is a powerful network toolbox for macOS & iOS. At its core, it works as a local proxy that lets you:

  • 🚀 Bypass network restrictions (via proxy nodes)
  • 🧠 Control traffic routing with rules
  • 🧪 Debug network requests (very strong feature)
  • 🔒 Enhance privacy and security
  • 📱 Manage proxies on Apple devices elegantly

In simple terms: Surge decides “which app / website goes through which proxy (or not)”

docs.title: 2. Surge vs Other Tools (Quick Comparison)
docs.text:
Tool Strength Weakness Clash Free, popular Limited rule flexibility Shadowrocket Easy on iOS Less powerful Surge 🔥 Most powerful Paid, learning curve

If you want fine-grained control and professional-grade rules, Surge is worth it.

docs.title: 3. Supported Platforms
docs.text:
• ✅ macOS (recommended for beginners)
  • ✅ iOS / iPadOS
  • ❌ Windows / Linux (not supported)

docs.title: 4. Core Concepts (Must Understand)
docs.text: Don’t skip this section 👇 Surge becomes easy once these are clear.

docs.title: 4.1 Proxy
docs.text:
A proxy is a server that forwards your traffic.

Examples:

  • Shadowsocks
  • Vmess
  • Trojan
  • HTTP / HTTPS

In Surge, proxies are called Proxy or Proxy Group.

docs.title: 4.2 Policy (Proxy Group)
docs.text:
A Policy decides which proxy to use.

Common types:

  • select → manually choose
  • url-test → auto choose fastest
  • fallback → backup system

Example:

ProxyGroup = select, 🇯🇵 JP, 🇺🇸 US, DIRECT

docs.title: 4.3 Rule
docs.text:
Rules decide:

Which traffic uses which policy

Examples:

  • Google → Proxy
  • Local websites → Direct
  • Ads → Block

Rule logic:

IF (condition) → THEN (policy)

docs.title: 4.4 DIRECT / REJECT
docs.text:
• DIRECT → no proxy, go straight
  • REJECT → block traffic

docs.title: 5. How Surge Works (Big Picture)
docs.text:
App → Surge → Rule → Policy → Proxy → Internet

Surge always follows this order.

docs.title: 6. Installing Surge (macOS)
docs.text:
1. Download from official site
  2. Install & open Surge
  3. Allow:
    • Network extension
    • VPN permission
  4. Status bar icon appears → Surge is running

docs.title: 7. Configuration File (.conf)
docs.text:
Surge uses one main config file.

Structure:

[General]
[Proxy]
[Proxy Group]
[Rule]

You usually subscribe instead of writing from scratch.

docs.title: 8.1 Import Subscription
docs.text:
1. Open Surge
  2. Profiles → Download Profile from URL
  3. Paste your provider’s subscription link
  4. Update profile

That’s it ✅

docs.title: 8.2 Profile Update
docs.text:
• Surge can auto-update
  • You can also manually refresh

docs.title: 9.1 [General]
docs.text:
Basic behavior settings:

[General]
loglevel = notify
dns-server = system

Beginners usually don’t touch this.

docs.title: 9.2 [Proxy]
docs.text:
Defines actual nodes.

Example:

[Proxy]
JP = ss, jp.example.com, 8388, encrypt-method=aes-256-gcm, password=123456

If you use subscriptions → auto generated.

docs.title: 9.3 [Proxy Group]
docs.text:
This is very important.

Example:

[Proxy Group]
Proxy = select, JP, US, DIRECT
Auto = url-test, JP, US, url=http://www.gstatic.com/generate_204

You usually use:

  • One manual group
  • One auto group

docs.title: 9.4 [Rule]
docs.text:
Rules are matched top → bottom.

Example:

[Rule]
DOMAIN-SUFFIX,google.com,Proxy
DOMAIN-SUFFIX,apple.com,DIRECT
GEOIP,CN,DIRECT
FINAL,Proxy

Meaning:

  1. Google → Proxy
  2. Apple → Direct
  3. China IP → Direct
  4. Everything else → Proxy

docs.title: 10. Rule Matching Priority ⚠️
docs.text:
Very important:

FIRST match wins

So:

  • Specific rules → top
  • General rules → bottom
  • FINAL → always last

docs.title: Simple & Safe Strategy
docs.text:
• Domestic websites → DIRECT
  • Foreign websites → Proxy
  • Auto node selection

This gives:

  • Good speed
  • Low maintenance

docs.title: 12. Surge Dashboard (macOS)
docs.text:
Key panels:

  • Overview → proxy status
  • Traffic → real-time connections
  • Requests → HTTP debugging
  • Rules → see matched rules

Surge is famous for its Request Inspector

docs.title: 13. Debugging with Surge (Bonus)
docs.text:
You can:

  • View HTTPS requests
  • Modify headers
  • Mock responses
  • Test APIs

This is why many developers love Surge.

docs.title: 14. Common Beginner Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Putting FINAL too early

❌ Mixing Clash rules directly

❌ Forgetting to enable Surge

❌ No DIRECT rules → slow local access

docs.title: 15. Learning Path (Recommended)
docs.text:
1. Use subscription (don’t write config)
  2. Learn:
    • Proxy Group
    • Rule logic
  3. Modify rules
  4. Learn Rewrite & Script (advanced)

docs.title: 16. When Should You Use Surge?
docs.text:
Use Surge if you want:

  • ✅ Precise routing control
  • ✅ Strong debugging
  • ✅ macOS / iOS ecosystem
  • ❌ Not free

docs.title: 17. Summary
docs.text:
• Surge = professional proxy controller
  • Rules decide where traffic goes
  • Policy decides which node to use
  • Beginners should start with subscriptions
  • Learn rules slowly → Surge becomes addictive 😄

docs.title: Apple Calendar
docs.text: Apple Calendar (formerly called iCal) is Apple’s built-in app for managing events, schedules, and reminders across all your Apple devices. It’s simple on the surface, but surprisingly powerful once you know the basics.

docs.title: 1. What Is Apple Calendar?
docs.text:
Apple Calendar lets you:

  • 📅 Create and manage events
  • 🔔 Set alerts and notifications
  • 🌍 Handle different time zones
  • 👥 Invite people to events
  • ☁️ Sync across iPhone, iPad, Mac, and web (via iCloud)
  • 🔗 Subscribe to shared or public calendars

It comes preinstalled on macOS, iOS, and iPadOS.

docs.title: On macOS
docs.text:
Main parts of the window:

  • Sidebar (left)
    • Calendar list (Work, Personal, Birthdays, etc.)
    • Shared and subscribed calendars
  • Calendar View (center)
    • Day / Week / Month / Year views
  • Toolbar (top)
    • Navigation arrows
    • View selector
    • “+” button to add events

docs.title: On iPhone / iPad
docs.text:
• Bottom tabs: Today / Calendars / Inbox / Search
  • Tap dates to view or add events

docs.title: On Mac
docs.text:
1. Open Calendar
  2. Double-click a date and time or click the “+” button
  3. Enter:
    • Event title
    • Time & duration
    • Location (optional)
  4. Click Done

docs.title: On iPhone / iPad
docs.text:
1. Open Calendar
  2. Tap + (top right)
  3. Fill in event details
  4. Tap Add

docs.title: 4. Editing and Deleting Events
docs.text:
• Edit: Click (or tap) an event → change details
  • Delete:
    • macOS: Select event → Delete
    • iOS: Open event → Delete Event

For repeating events, Apple Calendar will ask whether to delete:

  • This event only
  • This and future events
  • All events

docs.title: 5. Using Different Calendar Views
docs.text:
Apple Calendar supports multiple views:

  • Day – Hour-by-hour schedule
  • Week – Best for planning workloads
  • Month – Overview of busy days
  • Year (macOS) – Long-term planning

Switch views using the toolbar (Mac) or gestures/buttons (iOS).

docs.title: 6. Using Multiple Calendars (Very Important!)
docs.text:
You can create separate calendars for different purposes:

Examples:

  • 🧑‍💼 Work
  • 🏠 Personal
  • 🎓 Study
  • ✈️ Travel

docs.title: Create a New Calendar
docs.text:
• macOS: File → New Calendar
  • iOS: Calendars → Add Calendar

Each calendar can have its own color, making schedules easier to read.

docs.title: 7. Alerts & Notifications
docs.text:
Apple Calendar can remind you:

  • At the time of event
  • 5 minutes / 1 hour / 1 day before
  • Custom times

You can also:

  • Add multiple alerts
  • Use travel time alerts (based on Maps)

Great for meetings and deadlines ⏰

docs.title: 8. Inviting People to Events
docs.text:
You can invite others via email:

  1. Open an event
  2. Add invitees’ email addresses
  3. They receive an invitation
  4. Their response appears in your calendar

Works best when everyone uses Apple Calendar or iCloud.

docs.title: 9. iCloud Sync (One of the Best Features)
docs.text:
When iCloud is enabled:

  • Events sync automatically across devices
  • Changes appear almost instantly

docs.title: Enable iCloud Calendar
docs.text:
• macOS: System Settings → Apple ID → iCloud → Calendar
  • iOS: Settings → Apple ID → iCloud → Calendar

docs.title: 10. Subscribing to External Calendars
docs.text:
You can subscribe to:

  • Public holiday calendars
  • School or work schedules
  • Sports team calendars

docs.title: Subscribe on macOS
docs.text:
1. Calendar → File → New Calendar Subscription
  2. Paste the calendar URL (ICS)
  3. Choose update frequency

Subscribed calendars are read-only.

docs.title: Search
docs.text:
• Use the search bar to find events by:
    • Title
    • Location
    • Person

docs.title: Power Tips
docs.text:
• ⌨️ Type natural language: Meeting with Bob tomorrow at 3pm
  • 🌍 Enable time-zone support for travel
  • 🎂 Enable Birthdays calendar (from Contacts)
  • 🔁 Use recurring events for routines

docs.title: 12. Apple Calendar vs Reminders
docs.text:
• Calendar → time-based events
  • Reminders → tasks and to-dos

They work best together, not as replacements.

docs.title: 13. Who Is Apple Calendar Best For?
docs.text:
Perfect if you:

  • Use Apple devices daily
  • Want clean, native integration
  • Prefer simplicity over heavy customization
  • Rely on iCloud sync

docs.title: 14. Summary
docs.text:
Apple Calendar is:

  • ✅ Clean and fast
  • ✅ Deeply integrated with Apple ecosystem
  • ✅ Powerful enough for most daily scheduling
  • ❌ Limited for advanced project management

If you live in the Apple world, it’s one of the best calendars you can use.

docs.title: 1. What is ChatGPT?
docs.text:
ChatGPT is an AI assistant that understands natural language and responds in text.

You can think of it as:

  • 🧠 A smart conversation partner
  • 📚 A learning and explanation tool
  • ✍️ A writing and editing assistant
  • 💻 A coding and technical helper
  • 🛠️ A problem-solving tool

You talk to it in plain language, and it replies the same way.

docs.title: Common beginner use cases
docs.text:
Category Examples Learning Explain concepts, summarize articles, language learning Writing Emails, essays, notes, polishing text Coding Explain code, debug, write examples Productivity Plans, checklists, workflows Daily life Travel plans, fitness advice, cooking ideas

💡 Key idea: ChatGPT works best when you clearly describe what you want.

docs.title: 3. How to Use ChatGPT (Basic Workflow)
docs.text:
1. Type a question or request
  2. Press send
  3. Read the response
  4. Ask follow-up questions or refine

Example:

Explain Bluetooth in simple terms.

Follow-up:

Explain it again, but with real-world examples.

ChatGPT remembers context within the conversation, so you don’t need to repeat everything.

docs.title: 4. Prompts: The Most Important Concept
docs.text: Your input is called a prompt.

docs.title: Weak prompt ❌
docs.text: Explain Swift.

docs.title: Better prompt ✅
docs.text: Explain Swift for beginners with no programming background.

docs.title: Even better prompt ✅✅
docs.text:
Explain Swift for beginners. Use simple language, give examples, and avoid advanced concepts.

Rule of thumb

The clearer your prompt, the better the answer.

docs.title: 1️⃣ “Explain like I’m a beginner”
docs.text: Explain DNS like I’m a complete beginner.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Step-by-step
docs.text: Teach me how to learn IELTS listening step by step.

docs.title: 3️⃣ Ask for examples
docs.text: Give me examples and explain each one.

docs.title: 4️⃣ Ask for structure
docs.text: Create an outline before explaining.

docs.title: 5️⃣ Ask for simplification
docs.text: That’s too complex. Make it simpler.

docs.title: 6. ChatGPT Is Interactive (Use Follow-ups!)
docs.text:
You don’t need to get everything right in one prompt.

Example conversation:

User: Explain CSV files.
ChatGPT: (explains)
User: Focus more on macOS usage.
User: Give me a Swift example.

This is normal and encouraged.

docs.title: What ChatGPT is good at ✅
docs.text:
• Explaining concepts
  • Generating drafts
  • Brainstorming ideas
  • Learning assistance
  • Writing code examples

docs.title: What ChatGPT is NOT perfect at ⚠️
docs.text:
• Always being 100% correct
  • Real-time or breaking news
  • Professional legal/medical decisions
  • Knowing private or personal data

💡 Always double-check important facts.

docs.title: ✅ Do this
docs.text:
• Be specific
  • Ask follow-up questions
  • Ask for clarification
  • Ask for examples
  • Tell it your level (“beginner”, “intermediate”)

docs.title: ❌ Avoid this
docs.text:
• One-word prompts
  • Assuming it knows your goal
  • Treating answers as absolute truth

docs.title: 9. Example: A “Perfect” Beginner Prompt
docs.text:
I’m a beginner. Please explain how ChatGPT works,
using simple language, real examples,
and a clear structure.

This tells ChatGPT:

  • your level
  • the style you want
  • the format you prefer

docs.title: 10. How to Improve Quickly
docs.text:
Practice with:

  • “Explain X”
  • “Explain X again but simpler”
  • “Give me an example”
  • “Compare A and B”
  • “Summarize this text”

Within a few days, you’ll naturally learn how to prompt better.

docs.title: 11. Final Mindset Tip 🌱
docs.text:
ChatGPT is not a search engine and not a human.

It’s a tool — and like any tool, skill comes from use.

Treat it like a patient, knowledgeable assistant you can refine step by step.

docs.title: ChatGPT: Prompts
docs.text:
If you’ve ever typed something into ChatGPT and thought, “That’s not exactly what I meant…” — you’ve already discovered why prompt writing matters.

A prompt is simply the instruction or message you give to an AI system like ChatGPT. The better your prompt, the better the result.

This tutorial will teach you:

  1. What a prompt really is
  2. The basic structure of a good prompt
  3. Step-by-step methods for beginners
  4. Practical examples
  5. Advanced tips when you’re ready

docs.title: 1. What Is a Prompt?
docs.text:
A prompt is any input you give to ChatGPT.

Examples:

  • “Explain photosynthesis.”
  • “Write a professional email declining a job offer.”
  • “Summarize this article in 5 bullet points.”

Think of ChatGPT as:

  • Extremely knowledgeable
  • Very fast
  • But not a mind reader

If you are vague, the output will be vague. If you are precise, the output becomes precise.

docs.title: 2. The Core Principle: Clarity + Context + Constraints
docs.text: Great prompts usually include three elements:

docs.title: 1️⃣ Clarity (What do you want?)
docs.text:
Be explicit about the task.

Bad:

Tell me about history.

Better:

Explain the causes of World War I in simple terms.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Context (Why / For whom?)
docs.text:
Give background so ChatGPT understands your situation.

Instead of:

Write a speech about climate change.

Try:

Write a 3-minute speech about climate change for high school students. The tone should be persuasive but not aggressive.

docs.title: 3️⃣ Constraints (How should it look?)
docs.text:
Specify format, length, style, or structure.

Examples:

  • “In 5 bullet points”
  • “Under 200 words”
  • “Use simple vocabulary”
  • “Include examples”
  • “Make it formal”

docs.title: 3. The Basic Prompt Formula for Beginners
docs.text:
Use this simple structure:

Role + Task + Context + Format + Constraints

Let’s break it down.

docs.title: Step 1: Assign a Role (Optional but Powerful)
docs.text:
You can guide tone and expertise by assigning a role.

Examples:

  • “You are a marketing expert…”
  • “You are a high school teacher…”
  • “You are a cybersecurity specialist…”

This helps shape the style and depth.

docs.title: Step 2: Define the Task Clearly
docs.text:
Use strong action verbs:

  • Explain
  • Compare
  • Analyze
  • Summarize
  • Rewrite
  • Translate
  • Generate
  • Critique

Example:

Explain how blockchain works.

Better:

Explain how blockchain works in simple language for beginners.

docs.title: Step 3: Add Context
docs.text:
Provide details about:

  • Audience
  • Purpose
  • Your level
  • Situation

Example:

I’m preparing for an IELTS speaking test. Help me generate a Band 7-level answer to the topic “Describe a memorable trip.”

docs.title: Step 4: Specify the Output Format
docs.text:
Tell ChatGPT exactly how to structure the response.

Examples:

  • Bullet points
  • Table
  • Step-by-step guide
  • Email format
  • Code block
  • Dialogue
  • Checklist

Example:

Give me a comparison table between Python and JavaScript for beginners.

docs.title: 4. Examples: Bad Prompt vs Good Prompt
❌ Example 1
docs.text:
Bad:

Write about exercise.

Good:

Write a 300-word article about the benefits of daily exercise for office workers. Use simple language and include 3 practical tips.

docs.title: ❌ Example 2
docs.text:
Bad:

Help with my resume.

Good:

Rewrite this resume summary to sound more professional and achievement-oriented. Keep it under 120 words. Here is the text: [paste text]

docs.title: ❌ Example 3
docs.text:
Bad:

Explain AI.

Good:

Explain artificial intelligence to a 12-year-old using simple examples from daily life.

docs.title: 5. Use Examples Inside Your Prompt
docs.text:
If you want a specific style, show one.

Example:

Write 5 Instagram captions in this style: “Small steps today, big results tomorrow.”

This dramatically improves accuracy.

docs.title: 6. Iterative Prompting (Very Important)
docs.text:
You don’t need a perfect prompt the first time.

You can refine step by step:

  1. Ask broadly.
  2. Improve.
  3. Narrow it down.

Example flow:

You:

Give me business ideas.

Then:

Focus on low-cost online businesses.

Then:

Now only ideas suitable for a college student with programming skills.

This is how professionals use AI.

docs.title: ❌ Being Too Short
docs.text:
“Explain economics.”

Too broad → generic answer.

docs.title: ❌ Being Too Vague
docs.text:
“Make it better.”

Better:

Improve clarity and make it more persuasive.

docs.title: ❌ Forgetting the Audience
docs.text:
Different audiences require different language.

  • Kids
  • Experts
  • Customers
  • IELTS examiners
  • Investors

Always specify.

docs.title: 1️⃣ Ask for Structure First
docs.text:
Example:

Give me an outline first. After that, I will ask you to expand each section.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Ask for Multiple Options
docs.text: Give me 3 different tones: formal, friendly, and persuasive.

docs.title: 3️⃣ Ask for Self-Critique
docs.text: After writing the answer, evaluate it and suggest improvements.

docs.title: 4️⃣ Chain of Thought Guidance
docs.text:
Instead of:

Solve this math problem.

Try:

Solve this math problem step by step and explain your reasoning.

docs.title: 9. A Universal “Power Prompt” Template
docs.text:
Here is a template beginners can copy:

You are a [role].

Task:
[What you want done]

Context:
[Background information]

Requirements:
- Format:
- Length:
- Tone:
- Audience:
- Special instructions:

docs.title: 10. Final Advice
docs.text:
Think of ChatGPT as:

  • A very capable assistant
  • That follows instructions literally
  • And performs best with structured guidance

The quality of output = clarity of input.

If you improve your prompting skill, you improve:

  • Learning speed
  • Writing quality
  • Research efficiency
  • Coding productivity
  • Exam preparation

docs.title: 1. What problem does Docker solve?
docs.text:
Imagine this situation:

  • You write a program on your laptop ✅
  • You send it to a friend → ❌ “It doesn’t run”
  • You deploy it on a server → ❌ “Different OS, different versions”

Why?

Because software depends on:

  • OS
  • Libraries
  • Runtime (Python, Node, Java…)
  • Environment variables

👉 Docker solves this by packaging everything together.

Docker = “It runs the same everywhere.”

docs.title: 2. Docker in one sentence
docs.text:
Docker is a tool that packages an application and its environment into a container so it can run anywhere.

Key word: container

docs.title: Traditional Virtual Machine (VM)
docs.text:
• Runs a full OS
  • Heavy
  • Slow to start
  • High resource usage

docs.title: Docker Container
docs.text:
• Shares the host OS kernel
  • Lightweight
  • Starts in seconds (or milliseconds)
  • Uses much less memory

docs.title: Simple analogy
docs.text:
• VM = renting a whole house 🏠
  • Container = renting a furnished room 🛏️

docs.title: 1️⃣ Image
docs.text:
• A template
  • Read-only
  • Describes how to build the environment

Example:

ubuntu:22.04
nginx:latest
python:3.12

👉 Think of an image as a blueprint.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Container
docs.text:
• A running instance of an image
  • Can start, stop, delete

👉 Image = class

👉 Container = object

docs.title: 3️⃣ Dockerfile
docs.text:
• A recipe to build your own image
  • Text file

Example:

FROM python:3.12
COPY app.py /app.py
CMD ["python", "/app.py"]

docs.title: 4️⃣ Docker Hub
docs.text:
• Online image store
  • Like GitHub, but for Docker images

Example:

docker pull nginx

docs.title: macOS / Windows
docs.text:
• Install Docker Desktop
  • Includes:
    • Docker Engine
    • Docker CLI
    • Docker Compose

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
sudo apt install docker.io

Check:

docker --version

docs.title: Run a container
docs.text:
docker run hello-world

What happens:

  1. Docker checks if image exists locally
  2. If not → pulls from Docker Hub
  3. Creates a container
  4. Runs it
  5. Exits

🎉 Congratulations, Docker is working.

docs.title: 7. Running a real service (Nginx example)
docs.text:
docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx

Explain it word by word:

  • docker run → create + start container
  • -d → detached (run in background)
  • -p 8080:80 → map ports
    • host 8080 → container 80
  • nginx → image name

Visit:

http://localhost:8080

docs.title: List containers
docs.text:
docker ps
docker ps -a

docs.title: Stop container
docs.text: docker stop <container_id>

docs.title: Remove container
docs.text: docker rm <container_id>

docs.title: List images
docs.text: docker images

docs.title: Remove image
docs.text: docker rmi <image_id>

docs.title: 9. Volumes (data persistence)
docs.text:
Problem:

  • Container deleted → data gone ❌

Solution:

  • Volumes

Example:

docker run -v ./data:/data busybox

Meaning:

  • ./data (host)
  • /data (container)

👉 Data survives container deletion.

docs.title: 10. Docker Compose (multiple containers)
docs.text:
When you have:

  • App
  • Database
  • Cache

You don’t want 10 long docker run commands.

docs.title: docker-compose.yml example
docs.text:
services:
  web:
    image: nginx
    ports:
      - "8080:80"

Run:

docker compose up -d

Stop:

docker compose down

👉 One file to manage everything.

docs.title: 11. When should you use Docker?
docs.text:
✅ Use Docker when:

  • You want consistent environments
  • You deploy services
  • You use microservices
  • You hate “works on my machine”

❌ Don’t need Docker when:

  • Very simple scripts
  • Learning programming basics

docs.title: 12. Mental model
docs.text:
Docker is not magic.

It’s just:

  • Image → blueprint
  • Container → running process
  • Volume → data
  • Network → communication

Once you get this, Docker stops being scary.

docs.title: 13. What to learn next (recommended path)
docs.text:
1. Docker CLI basics ✅
  2. Dockerfile
  3. Volumes & networks
  4. Docker Compose
  5. Security & best practices

docs.title: 1. What Is Harbor?
docs.text: Harbor is an open-source, enterprise-grade container registry used to store, manage, and serve container images (Docker/OCI) and Helm charts. It is built on top of the standard Docker Registry but adds a lot of enterprise features you won’t find in the vanilla registry. (OneDPM)

docs.title: 🔑 Key Points
docs.text:
• Harbor stores container images and OCI artifacts (like Helm charts). (瑞恩笔记)
  • It provides a Web UI, access control & RBAC, audit logs, vulnerability scanning, and replication between registries. (OneDPM)
  • It’s widely used in DevOps/CICD pipelines in enterprises and internal infrastructure. (瑞恩笔记)

docs.title: 2. Why Use Harbor?
docs.text:
Compared with a simple Docker Registry:

✅ Web UI to browse images

✅ Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)

✅ LDAP/AD integration

✅ Vulnerability scanning (e.g., Trivy)

✅ Mirroring/replication between multiple Harbor instances

✅ Project-level isolation

✅ Helm chart repository support (瑞恩笔记)

These features make Harbor suitable for teams and enterprises that need secure and manageable image storage. (OneDPM)

docs.title: 3. Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before installing Harbor, make sure you have:

🔹 A VM/server with Linux (e.g., Ubuntu/CentOS)

🔹 Docker installed (Docker 20.10+ recommended)

🔹 docker-compose installed

🔹 40 GB+ disk space (more if you store lots of images) (王楚江)

docs.title: 4. Installing Harbor (Quick Guide)
docs.text: Harbor provides installers that automate deployment using Docker and docker-compose. Official docs cover a full install process. (Harbor)

docs.title: 1) Download the Harbor Installer
docs.text:
Go to the Harbor releases page on GitHub and fetch the latest version:

wget https://github.com/goharbor/harbor/releases/download/<version>/harbor-online-installer-<version>.tgz
tar -zxvf harbor-online-installer-<version>.tgz
cd harbor

docs.title: 2) Configure Harbor
docs.text:
Copy the sample config file:

cp harbor.yml.tmpl harbor.yml

Then edit harbor.yml:

  • Set your server’s hostname or IP under hostname:
  • Optionally set HTTPS certificates if you want secure access
  • Define the admin password (腾讯云)

docs.title: 3) Run the Installer
docs.text:
Once configured:

sudo ./install.sh

This generates docker-compose files and starts all Harbor microservices automatically. (腾讯云)

docs.title: 5. Logging Into Harbor
docs.text:
After installation completes:

  1. Open a browser to http://<your-host>:<port>
  2. Login with default credentials:
    • Username: admin
    • Password: what you set in harbor.yml (腾讯云)

docs.title: 6. Pushing and Pulling Images
docs.text: Once Harbor is up, you can push and pull container images just like any other registry.

docs.title: Example (replace with your host/project):
docs.text:
docker login <your-harbor-host>
docker pull nginx:latest
docker tag nginx:latest <your-harbor-host>/library/nginx:latest
docker push <your-harbor-host>/library/nginx:latest

If you’re using HTTP instead of HTTPS, you may need to mark the registry as insecure in your Docker daemon config (insecure-registries). (王楚江)

docs.title: 🗂 Projects & Repositories
docs.text: Harbor groups images into projects. Each project can be public or private and has fine-grained access control. (瑞恩笔记)

docs.title: 🔍 Vulnerability Scanning
docs.text: Harbor integrates scanners (Trivy, Clair) that analyze images for CVEs and report findings directly in the UI. (瑞恩笔记)

docs.title: 🔁 Replication
docs.text: Harbor can replicate images across multiple Harbor instances (useful for multi-region/high-availability setups). (瑞恩笔记)

docs.title: 8. Tips for Beginners
docs.text:
✅ Use HTTPS in production (prevents insecure registry issues). (Harbor)

✅ Back up Harbor’s PostgreSQL database and image storage regularly.

✅ Explore Harbor’s Web UI first — it’s a great way to understand projects and images visually.

✅ Integrate Harbor with your CI/CD pipelines (GitLab, GitHub Actions, etc.) for automated pushing.

docs.title: 9. Where to Learn More
docs.text:
✔ Official docs (install, admin, API, replication): https://goharbor.io/docs/ (Harbor)

✔ GitHub repo with installers and examples: https://github.com/goharbor/harbors

docs.title: 1. What is Home Assistant?
docs.text:
Home Assistant (HA) is an open-source smart home platform that lets you control and automate all your smart devices locally and privately.

In plain words:

Home Assistant = one brain for your smart home 🧠🏠

Instead of using:

  • Brand A app for lights
  • Brand B app for plugs
  • Brand C app for sensors

You use one dashboard and one automation system.

docs.title: ✅ Local first (fast & private)
docs.text:
• Automations run inside your home
  • Works even without internet
  • Your data stays with you

docs.title: ✅ Brand-agnostic
docs.text:
Supports thousands of devices:

  • Philips Hue
  • Xiaomi / Aqara
  • Tuya
  • IKEA
  • Sonoff
  • Shelly
  • Zigbee / Z-Wave devices

Mix brands freely. No lock-in.

docs.title: ✅ Extremely powerful automation
docs.text:
“If this happens → then do that → unless something else is true”

Example:

If motion is detected after sunset,

and I’m at home,

then turn on hallway light at 30% for 2 minutes.

docs.title: 🧩 Device integration
docs.text:
• Lights, switches, plugs
  • Temperature, humidity, motion
  • Door/window sensors
  • Cameras
  • TVs, speakers, AC

docs.title: ⚙️ Automation
docs.text:
• Time-based
  • Sensor-based
  • Event-based
  • Presence-based

docs.title: 📊 Dashboards
docs.text:
• Web UI
  • Mobile app (iOS / Android)
  • Fully customizable cards & layouts

docs.title: 🗣 Voice control
docs.text:
• Google Assistant
  • Alexa
  • Local voice assistants (advanced)

docs.title: 4. Typical Home Assistant architecture
docs.text:
[ Devices ]
   │
   ├── Wi-Fi
   ├── Zigbee
   ├── Z-Wave
   │
[ Home Assistant ]
   │
[ Dashboard / Automations ]

Key idea:

  • Home Assistant is the center
  • Devices talk to HA
  • HA decides what happens

docs.title: 5. How do people install Home Assistant?
Option 1: Home Assistant OS (best choice)
docs.text:
• Complete system
  • Web UI + add-ons + updates
  • Minimal Linux knowledge needed

Runs on:

  • Raspberry Pi
  • Intel NUC / Mini PC
  • Virtual machine

Think of it like “Home Assistant as an operating system”.

docs.title: Other options (for later)
docs.text:
• Docker
  • Supervised install
  • Python venv

As a beginner: don’t start here 🙂

docs.title: 6. First time experience
docs.text:
After installation, you access HA via browser:

http://homeassistant.local:8123

You’ll see:

  • Setup wizard
  • User creation
  • Auto-discovered devices

Home Assistant is very good at:

“Oh, I see a device on your network 👀

Want to add it?”

docs.title: 1️⃣ Entity
docs.text:
An entity is anything HA can control or read.

Examples:

  • light.living_room
  • sensor.temperature
  • switch.smart_plug

If it has a state → it’s an entity.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Device
docs.text:
A device is a physical thing.

One device → many entities.

Example:

A smart bulb may have:

  • Light entity
  • Power entity
  • Signal strength entity

docs.title: 3️⃣ Integration
docs.text:
An integration tells HA how to talk to something.

Examples:

  • Philips Hue integration
  • MQTT integration
  • Zigbee integration

No integration = no control.

docs.title: 4️⃣ Automation
docs.text:
An automation has three parts:

Trigger → Conditions → Actions

Example:

  • Trigger: Motion detected
  • Condition: After 10 PM
  • Action: Turn on light

docs.title: 8. Your first automation (example)
docs.text:
Goal: Turn on a light when motion is detected at night.

Logic:

  1. Motion sensor detects movement
  2. Time is after sunset
  3. Light turns on

This can be done:

  • Without writing code
  • Using HA’s visual automation editor

That’s a big win for beginners 🥳

docs.title: 9. Add-ons: superpowers for HA
docs.text:
Add-ons are extra services running next to HA.

Popular ones:

  • File Editor
  • MQTT broker
  • Zigbee2MQTT
  • Samba / SSH
  • Node-RED (visual automation)

Think:

Add-ons = plugins for your smart home brain

docs.title: 10. Zigbee & Z-Wave (quick intro)
docs.text: Many smart home devices are not Wi-Fi.

docs.title: Zigbee
docs.text:
• Low power
  • Mesh network
  • Very popular (Aqara, IKEA, Philips)

docs.title: Z-Wave
docs.text:
• More expensive
  • Very stable
  • Regional frequencies

Home Assistant supports both via USB dongles.

docs.title: 11. Is Home Assistant hard?
docs.text:
Short answer:

Easy to start, deep to master.

  • Day 1: basic control & automations
  • Week 1: dashboards & scenes
  • Month 1: advanced automations
  • Long term: full smart home logic 😎

You can go as simple or as crazy as you want.

docs.title: 12. Who should use Home Assistant?
docs.text:
Perfect if you:

  • Care about privacy
  • Hate vendor lock-in
  • Enjoy tinkering (even a little)
  • Want real automation, not just remote control

Maybe not ideal if:

  • You want “zero setup, zero thinking”
  • You’re fine with cloud-only apps

docs.title: 13. Final takeaway
docs.text:
If smart homes were computers:

  • Smart brand apps = calculators
  • Home Assistant = full operating system

Once you use it, it’s hard to go back 😉

docs.title: 0. What we’re deploying (important first)
docs.text:
On macOS with Docker, you cannot run Home Assistant OS. You will run:

✅ Home Assistant Container

That means:

  • ✔ Core HA features (dashboard, automations, integrations)
  • ❌ No “Supervisor / Add-ons” tab
  • ✔ Still very powerful (recommended for Mac users)

You can always migrate later to HA OS on a mini PC / NUC.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: • Mac mini M4 (Apple Silicon, ARM64)

docs.title: Software
docs.text:
• OrbStack (installed & running)
  • macOS user with admin rights

If OrbStack works and you can run Docker containers → you’re good.

docs.title: 2. Create a persistent data directory
docs.text:
Home Assistant must store data outside the container.

Open Terminal:

mkdir -p ~/docker/homeassistant

This directory will store:

  • Configuration
  • Automations
  • Database
  • Backups

If the container is deleted, your data stays.

docs.title: 3. Choose the correct Home Assistant image
docs.text:
For Apple Silicon:

  • Architecture: ARM64
  • Image: ghcr.io/home-assistant/home-assistant:stable

Good news 🎉

Home Assistant provides native ARM images, so no emulation needed.

docs.title: 4. Run Home Assistant using Docker (recommended way)
Option A: Docker CLI (simple & explicit)
docs.text:
docker run -d \
  --name homeassistant \
  --restart unless-stopped \
  --privileged \
  -e TZ=Asia/Taipei \
  -v ~/docker/homeassistant:/config \
  --network=host \
  ghcr.io/home-assistant/home-assistant:stable

docs.title: Explanation (important)
docs.text:
Option Meaning --name homeassistant Container name --restart unless-stopped Auto-start on boot --privileged Needed for integrations TZ=Asia/Shanghai Correct timezone -v ~/docker/homeassistant:/config Persistent data --network=host Best device discovery stable Stable HA version

⚠️ --network=host works perfectly in OrbStack (unlike Docker Desktop).

docs.title: 5. (Alternative) Deploy using Docker Compose
docs.text: If you prefer Compose (recommended long-term):

docs.title: Create docker-compose.yml
docs.text:
cd ~/docker/homeassistant
nano docker-compose.yml

services:
  homeassistant:
    container_name: homeassistant
    image: ghcr.io/home-assistant/home-assistant:stable
    restart: unless-stopped
    privileged: true
    network_mode: host
    environment:
      - TZ=Asia/Shanghai
    volumes:
      - ./config:/config

Then start it:

docker compose up -d

docs.title: 6. First boot (be patient)
docs.text:
Home Assistant takes 1–3 minutes on first start.

Check logs if curious:

docker logs -f homeassistant

Wait until you see something like:

Home Assistant initialized

docs.title: 7. Access Home Assistant
docs.text:
Open your browser:

http://localhost:8123

Or:

http://homeassistant.local:8123

You should see the Home Assistant onboarding screen 🎉

docs.title: 8. Initial setup (first time)
docs.text:
You’ll be guided to:

  1. Create a user
  2. Set location
  3. Set unit system
  4. Auto-discover devices

Home Assistant will immediately scan:

  • Network devices
  • Media players
  • Smart TVs
  • Routers
  • Some smart plugs

docs.title: ✅ Why OrbStack is great for HA
docs.text:
• Native Apple Silicon performance
  • Proper host networking
  • Low overhead
  • No weird mDNS issues (Bonjour works)

docs.title: ⚠️ USB devices (Zigbee / Z-Wave)
docs.text:
macOS cannot directly pass USB into Docker reliably.

Solutions:

  1. Use network-based coordinators (recommended)
    • Zigbee over Ethernet
    • Zigbee2MQTT on another machine
  2. Or run HA OS on dedicated hardware later

For Wi-Fi devices: no problem at all.

docs.title: 10. Updating Home Assistant (Docker way)
docs.text:
Very simple:

docker pull ghcr.io/home-assistant/home-assistant:stable
docker stop homeassistant
docker rm homeassistant

Then re-run the same docker run or:

docker compose up -d

Your config stays untouched.

docs.title: 11. Backup strategy (important!)
docs.text:
Since no Supervisor:

  • Your backup is simply ~/docker/homeassistant

You can:

  • Time Machine it
  • Sync it to NAS
  • Git version control (advanced)

docs.title: 12. Common beginner mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Forgetting volume mapping

→ All config lost after restart

❌ Using bridge network

→ Device discovery broken

❌ Expecting “Add-ons tab”

→ That’s HA OS only

docs.title: 13. When should you move off macOS?
docs.text:
Mac + Docker is perfect if:

  • You’re learning
  • Mostly Wi-Fi devices
  • Dashboard & automation focused

Move to HA OS if:

  • Heavy Zigbee/Z-Wave
  • 24/7 always-on server
  • Want Supervisor & Add-ons

Migration is painless later.

docs.title: 14. Final takeaway
docs.text:
M4 Mac mini + OrbStack + Docker gives you:

  • ⚡ Fast ARM-native performance
  • 🧼 Clean environment
  • 🧠 Full Home Assistant core features

It’s one of the best dev + learning setups for Home Assistant.

docs.title: 1. What is HACS?
docs.text:
HACS stands for Home Assistant Community Store.

Think of it as:

🏪 An app store for Home Assistant

With HACS, you can easily install:

  • Custom integrations (e.g. Xiaomi, iCloud, Govee, Tuya extras)
  • Custom Lovelace cards (better dashboards)
  • Themes (dark mode, minimal UI, iOS-style look)
  • Plugins made by the community

Without HACS, installing these usually means:

  • Manually copying files
  • Editing folders
  • Restarting HA multiple times

With HACS → one click install & update.

docs.title: 2. Do you really need HACS?
docs.text:
Short answer: Yes, if you want to level up Home Assistant.

You’ll want HACS if you:

  • Use community integrations not in official HA
  • Want better dashboards (Mushroom, Mini Graph Card, etc.)
  • Like clean, modern UI themes
  • Hate manual updates

If you only use official integrations → HACS is optional

But most HA power users cannot live without it 😉

docs.title: 3. Prerequisites (Before Installing)
docs.text:
Make sure you have:

✅ Home Assistant OS / Supervised / Container

❌ HACS does NOT work on Core (venv only)

Check:

Settings → About → Installation type

You also need:

  • Internet access
  • A Home Assistant user account (admin)

docs.title: Step 1: Enable Advanced Mode
docs.text:
1. Go to Settings → User Profile
  2. Enable Advanced Mode

This unlocks custom integrations.

docs.title: Step 2: Download HACS
docs.text:
Open Terminal / SSH in Home Assistant and run:

wget -O - https://get.hacs.xyz | bash -

This will:

  • Create /config/custom_components/hacs
  • Download HACS files automatically

docs.title: Step 3: Restart Home Assistant
docs.text:
Go to:

Settings → System → Restart

Wait until HA is fully back online.

docs.title: Step 4: Add HACS Integration
docs.text:
1. Go to Settings → Devices & Services
  2. Click Add Integration
  3. Search for HACS
  4. Follow the onboarding steps

You will be asked to:

  • Accept terms
  • Choose categories (Integrations, Frontend, Themes)

docs.title: Step 5: GitHub Authorization (Important)
docs.text:
HACS uses GitHub API.

You will:

  1. Be shown a GitHub verification code
  2. Open a link
  3. Login to GitHub
  4. Paste the code

👉 No repo access needed

👉 Public GitHub account is enough

docs.title: 5. Where to Find HACS After Installation?
docs.text:
After success, you’ll see:

Sidebar → HACS

Inside HACS you’ll find sections like:

  • Integrations
  • Frontend
  • Themes
  • Automations (optional)

docs.title: 6. Install Your First Thing with HACS
Example: Install a Custom Integration
docs.text:
1. Open HACS
  2. Go to Integrations
  3. Click Explore & Download Repositories
  4. Search an integration (e.g. Govee, Xiaomi, iCloud)
  5. Click Download
  6. Restart Home Assistant
  7. Add it via Settings → Devices & Services

docs.title: Example: Install a Lovelace Card
docs.text:
1. HACS → Frontend
  2. Search: Mushroom
  3. Download
  4. Restart HA
  5. Add card in Dashboard UI

✨ Much nicer UI instantly

docs.title: 7. Updating with HACS
docs.text:
This is where HACS shines.

  • Updates appear automatically in HACS
  • One click → update
  • No manual file handling

You’ll often see:

🔔 HACS → Updates available

docs.title: 8. HACS vs Official Integrations
docs.text:
Feature Official HA HACS Stability ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ ⭐⭐⭐ New features Slow Very fast Community plugins ❌ ✅ One-click updates ✅ ✅

💡 Best practice:

  • Prefer official when possible
  • Use HACS when official doesn’t exist

docs.title: 9. Common Beginner Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Forgetting to restart after install

❌ Installing but not adding integration

❌ Using Core install (HACS unsupported)

❌ Missing GitHub auth step

docs.title: 10. Is HACS Safe?
docs.text:
Yes, if you are careful:

  • HACS itself is widely trusted
  • Integrations are community-made
  • Always check:
    • Stars
    • Last update
    • README

If something breaks → disable it and restart.

docs.title: 11. Recommended HACS Picks for Beginners
docs.text:
🔥 Integrations

  • Xiaomi Miot
  • iCloud3
  • Govee
  • LocalTuya

🎨 Frontend / Cards

  • Mushroom
  • Mini Graph Card
  • Button Card

🎭 Themes

  • Mushroom Theme
  • iOS Theme
  • Minimalist

docs.title: 12. Final Thoughts
docs.text:
If Home Assistant is the operating system of your smart home, then HACS is the app store that makes it powerful and fun.

Once you install HACS:

You’ll never want to manage custom integrations manually again 😄

docs.title: 1. What is Google Chrome?
docs.text:
Google Chrome is a fast, secure, and widely used web browser developed by Google. It allows you to access websites, web apps, and online services. Key features include:

  • Speed – Chrome loads pages quickly.
  • Security – Built-in protections against malware and phishing.
  • Extensions – Add extra functions via the Chrome Web Store.
  • Cross-platform – Works on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, and iOS.
  • Sync – Sync bookmarks, history, and passwords across devices with a Google account.

docs.title: On Windows or macOS:
docs.text:
1. Go to https://www.google.com/chrome/
  2. Click Download Chrome.
  3. Open the downloaded installer and follow the instructions.
  4. Launch Chrome from your desktop or Applications folder.

docs.title: On Linux (Ubuntu example):
docs.text:
wget https://dl.google.com/linux/direct/google-chrome-stable_current_amd64.deb
sudo dpkg -i google-chrome-stable_current_amd64.deb
sudo apt-get install -f   # Fix missing dependencies

docs.title: On Mobile:
docs.text:
• Android: Install from Google Play Store.
  • iOS: Install from App Store.

docs.title: 3. Chrome Interface Basics
docs.text:
1. Address Bar (Omnibox) – Type URLs or search terms here.
  2. Tabs – Open multiple websites in the same window.
  3. Back / Forward Buttons – Navigate your browsing history.
  4. Reload Button – Refresh the current page.
  5. Bookmarks Bar – Quickly access your favorite websites.
  6. Menu (⋮) – Access settings, extensions, history, downloads, and more.

docs.title: 4. Managing Tabs and Windows
docs.text:
• Open a new tab: Ctrl+T (Windows) / Cmd+T (Mac)
  • Open a new window: Ctrl+N / Cmd+N
  • Open a private/incognito window: Ctrl+Shift+N / Cmd+Shift+N
  • Move tabs between windows: Drag and drop the tab.
  • Pin tabs to save space: Right-click tab → Pin Tab

docs.title: 5. Bookmarks and History
docs.text:
• Add a bookmark:
    • Click ⭐ in the Omnibox.
    • CMD + D
  • Organize bookmarks:
    • Menu → Bookmarks → Bookmark Manager
    • CMD + Option + B
    • chrome://bookmarks
  • Show or hide bookmarks: CMD + SHIFT + B
  • View history: Ctrl+H / Cmd+Y.
  • Search history: Use the search bar in the history page.

docs.title: 6. Chrome Extensions
docs.text:
Extensions are mini-apps that enhance Chrome’s functionality.

  • Install: Visit Chrome Web Store → Click Add to Chrome.
  • Manage extensions:
    • Menu → More Tools → Extensions
    • chrome://extensions/
  • Examples of useful extensions:
    • Grammarly – Grammar and spell check.
    • AdBlock – Block ads.
    • LastPass – Password manager.
    • Dark Reader – Dark mode for websites.
    • More: https://guokai.dev/

docs.title: 7. Chrome Settings
docs.text:
• Access: Menu → Settings.
  • Privacy and Security:
    • Clear browsing data.
    • Control cookies and site permissions.
    • Safe Browsing.
  • Appearance:
    • Theme, font size, and show/hide bookmarks bar.
  • Default Browser:
    • Set Chrome as your default browser.

docs.title: 8. Chrome Tips for Beginners
docs.text:
1. Keyboard Shortcuts:
    • Ctrl+T / Cmd+T → New tab
    • Ctrl+Shift+T / Cmd+Shift+T → Reopen closed tab
    • Ctrl+W / Cmd+W → Close current tab
    • Ctrl+Tab → Switch to next tab
    • Ctrl+Shift+Tab → Switch to previous tab
    • more: https://support.google.com/chrome/answer/157179
  2. Sync across devices:
    • Sign in with your Google account → Sync bookmarks, passwords, history.
  3. Pin favorite websites:
    • Right-click tab → Pin Tab → Tabs become smaller and stay in place.
  4. Incognito mode:
    • Browsing without saving history or cookies.
  5. Chrome task manager:
    • Menu → More Tools → Task Manager → Monitor CPU & memory usage of tabs and extensions.

docs.title: 9. Using Chrome Efficiently
docs.text:
• Search directly from the Omnibox: Type a question or keyword → Press Enter.
  • Drag URLs to the bookmarks bar for quick access.
  • Right-click images/videos → Save or copy URL.
  • Use multiple profiles: Menu → Profile → Add → Separate work/personal accounts.

docs.title: 10. Safety Tips
docs.text:
• Only install extensions from trusted sources.
  • Keep Chrome updated for security patches.
  • Avoid clicking suspicious links or downloads.

Chrome is beginner-friendly, but mastering bookmarks, extensions, and keyboard shortcuts can make browsing much faster and enjoyable.

docs.title: Bilibili Player
docs.text:
Extension for Bilibili Player is a Chrome extension that enhances the Bilibili web video player by adding powerful keyboard shortcuts, better default behaviors, and extra viewing features. It is especially useful if you prefer keyboard control or watch long videos regularly.

Chrome Web Store: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/extension-for-bilibili-pl/ffoljpljalicgkljioegejmigkkkincm

docs.title: 1️⃣ What Does This Extension Do?
docs.text:

  4. (Optional) Pin the extension from the browser toolbar for quick access.

docs.title: 3️⃣ Default Behavior (Out of the Box)

  • Automatically applies preferred display modes

docs.title: 5️⃣ Extension Settings (Customization)
docs.text:
To open settings:

  1. Click the extension icon in the browser toolbar
  2. Select Options / Settings

You can:

  • Enable or disable specific shortcuts
  • Change seek time (short / long jumps)
  • Adjust playback speed step size
  • Disable features you don’t use
  • Avoid conflicts with browser or system shortcuts

⚠️ Refresh the Bilibili page after changing settings.

docs.title: 6️⃣ Tips for Beginners
docs.text:
• Start with Space, J, L, F, D — these cover 90% of use cases
  • Disable shortcuts you never use to avoid conflicts
  • Use PiP mode (P) when multitasking
  • Turn off danmaku by default if you watch lectures or tutorials
  • Frame-by-frame mode is great for animation or technical videos

docs.title: 7️⃣ What This Extension Does Not Do
docs.text:
• It does not download videos
  • It does not bypass Bilibili restrictions
  • It does not require a Bilibili account
  • It only enhances the web player experience

docs.title: 8️⃣ Who Is This Extension For?
docs.text:
✔ Heavy Bilibili users

✔ Keyboard-driven users

✔ Learners watching long courses

✔ Users who want YouTube-like controls on Bilibili

docs.title: Trancy
docs.text: A simple guide to learning languages with videos

docs.title: 1. What is Trancy?
docs.text:
Trancy is a browser extension designed to help you learn languages—especially English—by watching videos.

It works mainly with:

  • YouTube
  • Netflix (paid plans)
  • Other subtitle-supported video platforms

Trancy adds powerful learning features on top of videos, such as:

  • Dual subtitles
  • Word lookup
  • Sentence translation
  • Vocabulary collection

You learn naturally while watching content you enjoy.

docs.title: 2. Who is Trancy for?
docs.text:
Trancy is suitable for:

  • Beginners learning English
  • Students preparing for exams (IELTS, TOEFL, CET)
  • People improving listening and vocabulary
  • Anyone who learns better through videos

No technical background is required.

docs.title: 3. How Trancy Works (Core Idea)
docs.text:
The idea is simple:

Watch → Read subtitles → Click words → Understand → Remember

Instead of passively watching videos, Trancy turns them into interactive learning material.

docs.title: Step 1: Choose a Browser
docs.text:
Trancy works best on:

  • Chrome
  • Edge
  • Brave

docs.title: Step 2: Install the Extension
docs.text:
1. Open your browser’s extension store
  2. Search for “Trancy”
  3. Click Add to browser
  4. Pin Trancy to the toolbar (recommended)

That’s it—no complex setup.

docs.title: 5. First Time Setup
docs.text:
After installation:

  1. Click the Trancy icon
  2. Select your learning language (e.g. English)
  3. Select your native language (e.g. Chinese)

Trancy will now translate subtitles into your native language.

docs.title: Step 1: Open a YouTube Video
docs.text:
Choose a video that:

  • Has English subtitles
  • Is not too fast (talk shows, vlogs, interviews are great)

docs.title: Step 2: Enable Trancy
docs.text:
• Trancy activates automatically
  • You’ll see dual subtitles appear

Example:

English subtitle
Chinese translation

docs.title: 1️⃣ Dual Subtitles
docs.text:
• Shows English + translation
  • Helps you understand meaning instantly
  • Reduces the need to pause the video

Best for beginners.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Click-to-Translate Words
docs.text:
• Click any word in the subtitle
  • See:
    • Meaning
    • Pronunciation
    • Example usage

This is much faster than using a dictionary.

docs.title: 3️⃣ Sentence Translation
docs.text:
• Hover over a sentence
  • See the full translated meaning
  • Useful for complex grammar or long sentences

docs.title: 4️⃣ Replay Sentence / Loop
docs.text:
• Replay a single sentence
  • Improve listening and pronunciation
  • Very useful for shadowing practice

docs.title: 5️⃣ Vocabulary Collection
docs.text:
• Save words you don’t know
  • Build your personal word list
  • Review later

Think of it as video-based Anki, but simpler.

docs.title: 8. Recommended Learning Workflow (Beginner)
docs.text:
Here’s a simple routine:

  1. Play a video you like
  2. Watch with dual subtitles
  3. Click unfamiliar words
  4. Save important words
  5. Replay difficult sentences
  6. Don’t try to understand everything

15–30 minutes per day is enough.

docs.title: 9. Tips for Beginners
docs.text:
• ✅ Choose slow, clear speakers
  • ✅ Watch content you already like
  • ❌ Don’t pause every sentence
  • ❌ Don’t memorize everything at once
  • ✅ Focus on high-frequency words

Consistency is more important than speed.

docs.title: 10. Free vs Paid
docs.text:
• Free version: Enough for beginners
  • Paid version:
    • Netflix support
    • More advanced features
    • Better for long-term learners

You can start free and upgrade later.

docs.title: 11. Trancy vs Traditional Learning
docs.text: Traditional Trancy Textbooks Real videos Isolated words Context-based Boring Engaging Passive Interactive

docs.title: 12. Summary
docs.text:
Trancy is:

  • Easy to use
  • Video-based
  • Beginner-friendly
  • Great for listening & vocabulary

If you like watching videos and want to learn English naturally, Trancy is an excellent tool.

docs.text: • 《柯林斯双解》for macOS

docs.title: 1. What Is Eudic?
docs.text:
Eudic (欧路词典) is a powerful multilingual dictionary and language-learning tool, especially popular among English learners, translators, and students.

It goes far beyond a simple “word lookup” app by combining:

  • High-quality dictionaries
  • Offline lookup
  • Vocabulary management (word lists, review)
  • Example sentences and corpora
  • Deep integration with macOS, iOS, and Windows

You can think of Eudic as:

Dictionary + Vocabulary notebook + Reading assistant

docs.title: 2. Platforms and Versions
docs.text:
Eudic is available on:

  • macOS (desktop app)
  • Windows
  • iOS / iPadOS
  • Android

Key idea:

  • Mobile → quick lookup & memorization
  • Desktop → deep reading, writing, and research

Accounts can sync data (word lists, notes) across devices.

docs.title: 3. Core Concept: “Lookup First, Learn Later”
docs.text:
Eudic is built around a simple but powerful workflow:

  1. Look up a word
  2. Understand it in context
  3. Save it if necessary
  4. Review it later

This separation keeps lookup fast and learning systematic.

docs.title: 4.1 Searching a Word
docs.text:
You can search by:

  • English word (e.g. clarify)
  • Phrase (e.g. in the long run)
  • Inflected form (went → go)
  • Partial input (auto-completion)

Results usually include:

  • Phonetics (IPA / American / British)
  • Multiple definitions
  • Parts of speech
  • Example sentences

docs.title: 4.2 Pronunciation
docs.text:
Eudic supports:

  • British / American pronunciation
  • Offline TTS
  • Online audio (if enabled)

Tip:

Use pronunciation buttons actively—don’t just read silently.

docs.title: 5.1 Built-in Dictionaries
docs.text:
Eudic comes with:

  • English–Chinese dictionaries
  • English–English dictionaries
  • Collocation and example dictionaries

docs.title: 5.2 Importing Dictionaries (Advanced)
docs.text:
You can import:

  • MDX / MDict dictionaries
  • Specialized dictionaries (IELTS, TOEFL, medical, legal)

This is one of Eudic’s strongest features.

docs.title: 6.1 Word Lists (生词本)
docs.text:
When you click “Add to Word List”:

  • The word is saved
  • You can add notes or tags
  • It becomes part of your learning system

Think of word lists as:

Your personal dictionary, not a random collection

docs.title: 6.2 Multiple Word Lists
docs.text:
You can create lists for:

  • IELTS
  • Academic reading
  • Programming / technical English
  • Daily reading

Organize by purpose, not by difficulty.

docs.title: 7. Reviewing Words
docs.text:
Eudic includes built-in review modes:

  • Flashcard-style review
  • Spaced repetition (basic)
  • Word → meaning
  • Meaning → word

Best practice:

  • Review little and often
  • Don’t overload one list

docs.title: 8. Example Sentences & Corpora
docs.text:
Eudic shines at contextual learning.

You can:

  • See real example sentences
  • Compare different usages
  • Observe collocations and patterns

Instead of memorizing:

“word = meaning”

You learn:

“word = usage + structure + tone”

docs.title: 9.1 Built-in Reading
docs.text:
On desktop and mobile, you can:

  • Paste text
  • Open articles
  • Tap / hover to look up words instantly

This makes Eudic a reading companion, not just a dictionary.

docs.title: 9.2 Copy & Hover (Desktop)
docs.text:
On macOS / Windows:

  • Enable clipboard or hover lookup
  • Instantly see definitions while reading PDFs, browsers, or editors

docs.title: 10. Notes, Tags, and Custom Fields
docs.text:
For each word, you can add:

  • Personal notes
  • Example sentences
  • Tags (e.g. formal, spoken, academic)

This turns Eudic into a mini knowledge base for vocabulary.

docs.title: 11. Sync and Backup
docs.text:
• Log in to an Eudic account
  • Enable cloud sync
  • Word lists and notes sync across devices

Always ensure:

  • Sync is enabled
  • Periodic backups (especially on desktop)

docs.title: 12. Who Should Use Eudic?
docs.text:
Eudic is ideal if you:

  • Learn English seriously
  • Read a lot of English content
  • Prepare for exams (IELTS, TOEFL, CET)
  • Translate or write professionally

If you only need:

  • Very casual word lookup → Eudic may feel “too powerful”

docs.title: 13. Recommended Learning Workflow
docs.text:
A simple, effective routine:

  1. Read English content
  2. Look up unknown words in Eudic
  3. Save only useful words
  4. Add short notes or examples
  5. Review regularly

Consistency beats complexity.

docs.title: 14. Final Thoughts
docs.text:
Eudic is not just a dictionary—it’s a language learning system.

If you:

  • Use it lightly → it’s a fast dictionary
  • Use it deeply → it becomes a long-term language partner

Once set up well, it can support you for years of learning.
