docs.title: 1. What Is GoldenDict?
docs.text:
GoldenDict is a free, open-source, cross-platform dictionary application for Windows, macOS, and Linux.

Its core philosophy is very clear:

GoldenDict itself provides no content — you bring your own dictionaries.

Because of this, GoldenDict is extremely popular among:

  • Advanced language learners
  • Translators
  • Researchers
  • Users who want maximum control over dictionaries

docs.title: 2. How GoldenDict Is Different
docs.text:
Unlike online or “all-in-one” dictionaries:

Feature GoldenDict Built-in dictionaries ❌ None Offline usage ✅ Fully offline Dictionary formats ✅ Many Customization ✅ Very high Learning / memorization ❌ Minimal

GoldenDict is best thought of as:

A dictionary engine, not a learning app

docs.title: 3. Supported Platforms
docs.text:
GoldenDict runs on:

  • Windows
  • macOS
  • Linux

Data is stored locally.

No account, no cloud, no forced sync.

docs.title: 4. Supported Dictionary Formats
docs.text:
GoldenDict supports many formats, including:

  • MDict / MDX
  • StarDict
  • Lingvo DSL
  • Babylon
  • Plain text (limited)

This makes it ideal if you already own or collect dictionary files.

docs.title: 5. First Launch Overview
docs.text:
When you open GoldenDict for the first time, you’ll see:

  • A search box at the top
  • An empty or minimal result panel
  • No useful results yet (this is normal!)

GoldenDict is not usable until you add dictionaries.

docs.title: 6.1 Prepare Dictionary Files
docs.text:
Typical structure:

  • A folder containing .mdx, .dict, .idx, .ifo, etc.
  • Do not rename internal files

Example:

Dictionaries/
 ├── Oxford/
 ├── Longman/
 └── Collins/

docs.title: 6.2 Add Dictionary Paths
docs.text:
1. Open Preferences
  2. Go to Dictionaries
  3. Add the folder path containing your dictionaries
  4. Click Rescan

GoldenDict will:

  • Detect supported dictionaries
  • Index them automatically

docs.title: 7.1 Searching Words
docs.text:
• Type a word → press Enter
  • Results appear grouped by dictionary
  • Scroll to compare definitions

GoldenDict does not merge meanings — it shows raw dictionary outputs.

This is a feature, not a flaw.

docs.title: 8. Scan Popup (Extremely Useful)
docs.text:
GoldenDict supports Scan Popup:

  • Select a word in any app
  • Press a shortcut key
  • A small popup window shows definitions

Typical use cases:

  • Reading PDFs
  • Browsing articles
  • Coding documentation

This turns GoldenDict into a system-wide dictionary.

docs.title: 9. Pronunciation Support
docs.text:
GoldenDict can:

  • Play embedded pronunciation audio
  • Use external TTS engines

However:

  • Quality depends on the dictionary
  • No unified pronunciation system

If pronunciation matters a lot, choose dictionaries carefully.

docs.title: 10. Dictionary Groups
docs.text:
You can create dictionary groups:

Examples:

  • English–English
  • English–Chinese
  • Technical
  • Academic

Each group can be enabled or disabled with one click.

This avoids information overload.

docs.title: 11. Search Features
docs.text:
GoldenDict supports:

  • Fuzzy search
  • Wildcards (*, ?)
  • Full-text search (dictionary-dependent)

Useful when:

  • You’re unsure of spelling
  • You remember only part of a word

docs.title: 12. Styling and Display
docs.text:
GoldenDict allows:

  • Font customization
  • Dark / light themes
  • CSS-like formatting (advanced)

Result appearance depends heavily on:

  • Dictionary formatting quality
  • User settings

docs.title: 13. What GoldenDict Does Not Do
docs.text:
GoldenDict intentionally does not provide:

  • Word lists
  • Spaced repetition
  • Flashcards
  • Cloud sync
  • Learning statistics

GoldenDict focuses on:

Fast, accurate reference — nothing else

docs.title: 14. Ideal Use Cases
docs.text:
GoldenDict is perfect if you:

  • Want full offline control
  • Use many professional dictionaries
  • Read a lot on desktop
  • Prefer raw, unfiltered definitions

It is not ideal if you:

  • Want built-in memorization
  • Learn casually on mobile
  • Prefer polished UI over flexibility

docs.title: 15. GoldenDict + Other Tools
docs.text:
Many advanced users combine:

  • GoldenDict → lookup
  • Anki → memorization
  • Eudic → mobile learning

GoldenDict becomes the lookup engine, not the learning center.

docs.title: 16. Recommended Workflow
docs.text:
A simple professional workflow:

  1. Read on desktop
  2. Look up words via Scan Popup
  3. Understand using multiple dictionaries
  4. Manually record important words elsewhere (if needed)

GoldenDict stays fast because it stays focused.

docs.title: 17. Final Thoughts
docs.text:
GoldenDict is not beginner-friendly by default — but once configured, it’s one of the most powerful dictionary tools available.

If you value:

  • Ownership
  • Offline access
  • Precision
  • Customization

GoldenDict is hard to beat.

docs.title: 1. What Anki Is (and What It Is Not)
docs.text:
Anki is a spaced repetition flashcard system.

  • It helps you remember information for years, not days.
  • It is optimized for long-term memory, not short-term cramming.
  • It is used by:
    • Language learners
    • Medical students
    • Programmers
    • Exam candidates (IELTS, GRE, 408, etc.)

❌ Anki is not:

  • A note-taking app
  • A mind map tool
  • A place to dump textbooks

Think of Anki as a memory trainer, not a notebook.

docs.title: 2. The Core Idea: Spaced Repetition
docs.text:
Human memory follows a forgetting curve:

  • You forget most information quickly
  • Unless you review it at the right time

Anki solves this by:

  • Showing you a card just before you forget it
  • Increasing the interval each time you remember it

Example:

Day 1 → Day 3 → Day 8 → Day 25 → Day 90 → …

You don’t choose when to review.

Anki decides for you.

docs.title: 3.1 Card
docs.text:
A card is one test of memory.

Examples:

  • Front: “What is DHCP?”
  • Back: “Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol…”

One fact → one card.

docs.title: 3.2 Note vs Card (Common Beginner Mistake)
docs.text:
• Note: raw data you enter
  • Card: questions generated from the note

Example (Language learning):

Note:

Word: abandon
Meaning: give up

Cards generated:

  • English → Chinese
  • Chinese → English
  • Cloze sentence

👉 One note can create multiple cards.

docs.title: 3.3 Deck
docs.text:
A deck is a collection of cards.

Examples:

  • English Vocabulary
  • Computer Networks
  • Operating Systems
  • IELTS Listening

Rule of thumb:

  • Decks = topics
  • Cards = atomic knowledge

docs.title: 4. How Anki Testing Actually Works
docs.text: When reviewing, Anki asks a question and gives you buttons:

docs.title: Common Buttons (Default)
docs.text:
• Again – I forgot
  • Hard – I barely remembered
  • Good – normal recall
  • Easy – too easy

What happens:

  • Again → card comes back soon
  • Good → interval increases
  • Easy → interval increases more

👉 Be honest.

Anki only works if you don’t lie to yourself.

docs.title: 5. The Most Important Rule: Atomic Cards
docs.text:
One card = one idea

Bad card ❌:

Explain TCP, UDP, and their differences

Good cards ✅:

What is TCP?
What is UDP?
One key difference between TCP and UDP?

Why:

  • Your brain recalls small facts better
  • Anki schedules more accurately

docs.title: 6.1 Basic (Front / Back)
docs.text:
Best for:

  • Definitions
  • Concepts
  • Simple facts

Example:

Front: What is NAT?
Back: Network Address Translation

docs.title: 6.2 Cloze Deletion (Very Powerful)
docs.text:
You hide part of a sentence.

Example:

TCP is a {{c1::connection-oriented}} protocol.

Why cloze is powerful:

  • Context is preserved
  • Faster to create
  • Very effective for technical subjects

docs.title: 6.3 Multiple Choice (Use Carefully)
docs.text:
Good for:

  • Exam-style recognition

Bad for:

  • Real understanding (too easy to guess)

If you use MC:

  • Keep options meaningful
  • Avoid obvious distractors

docs.title: Step 1: Learn outside Anki
docs.text:
• Book
  • Lecture
  • Video
  • Practice

👉 Anki is not for first exposure.

docs.title: Step 2: Create Cards
docs.text:
Ask:

  • “What do I want future-me to remember?”
  • “What might I forget?”

docs.title: Step 3: Daily Review (Non-Negotiable)
docs.text:
• 10–30 minutes per day
  • Never skip multiple days

Anki rewards consistency, not intensity.

docs.title: 8. Settings You Should Understand (But Not Over-Tweak)
docs.text:
Beginner advice:

Default settings are good enough.

Only adjust:

  • New cards per day (start small: 10–20)
  • Review limit (keep it manageable)

Avoid:

  • Random add-ons
  • Extreme interval changes
  • Copying “ultimate settings” online

docs.title: 9. Anki on Multiple Devices
docs.text:
Typical setup:

  • Desktop: create cards
  • Mobile: review anytime

Sync uses AnkiWeb.

Important rule:

  • Sync before and after each session

docs.title: 10. Common Beginner Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Making cards too long

❌ Copying slides verbatim

❌ Adding hundreds of cards per day

❌ Skipping reviews

❌ Using Anki as a notebook

If Anki feels painful:

  • Cards are probably too big
  • Or reviews were skipped

docs.title: 11. What Anki Is Best At
docs.text:
Excellent for:

  • Vocabulary
  • Formulas
  • Definitions
  • Laws, rules, commands
  • Key concepts in CS / medicine / exams

Not ideal for:

  • Open-ended essays
  • Creative writing
  • Deep reasoning alone (use practice + Anki)

docs.title: 12. Mental Model to Remember
docs.text:
Learn → distill → test → repeat

Anki is the testing engine of your brain.

If used correctly:

  • You study less
  • You remember more
  • You stop re-learning the same things

docs.title: Anki: Design
docs.text:
How Anki Thinks About Memory

Anki is not just a flashcard app.

It is the practical implementation of how human memory works.

To use Anki well, you must think like Anki.

docs.title: 1. Anki Optimizes for Long-Term Memory, Not Comfort
docs.text:
Most study tools optimize for:

  • Feeling productive
  • Reading a lot
  • Highlighting a lot

Anki optimizes for:

  • Retention after months or years

This leads to uncomfortable design choices:

  • You are forced to recall, not reread
  • You see cards you’d rather avoid
  • You cannot “finish” Anki forever

👉 Anki assumes:

If it feels easy, you’re probably not learning.

docs.title: Passive review does not create memory
docs.text:
• Reading → weak memory
  • Recognition → illusion of knowledge
  • Recall → strong memory

Anki’s core rule:

Every review must be a question.

That’s why:

  • Cards have fronts and backs
  • Answers are hidden
  • You must commit before seeing the answer

If a card does not force recall, it violates Anki’s philosophy.

docs.title: 3. Forgetting Is a Feature, Not a Bug
docs.text:
Most learners fear forgetting.

Anki expects it.

Memory works like this:

  • Forget a bit → recall → memory strengthens
  • Never forget → memory stays weak

So Anki:

  • Waits until you are about to forget
  • Tests you at that moment
  • Adjusts timing based on your failure

👉 Forgetting tells Anki when to show a card again.

docs.title: 4. Time Is the Most Valuable Resource
docs.text:
Anki treats your time as scarce.

Design consequences:

  • Short cards are favored
  • Overloaded cards are punished
  • Bad cards create review explosions

Anki’s hidden assumption:

One idea should take a few seconds to recall.

If a card takes 30 seconds:

  • It breaks scheduling
  • It increases fatigue
  • It reduces long-term consistency

docs.title: 5. One Card = One Decision
docs.text:
Each review asks one question:

“Do you know this right now?”

No partial credit.

No explanations.

No debate.

That’s why buttons are simple:

  • Again
  • Hard
  • Good
  • Easy

Anki does not ask:

  • Why you forgot
  • How you reasoned
  • What confused you

It only cares about:

Was recall successful or not?

docs.title: 6. Notes Are Inputs, Cards Are Outputs
docs.text:
This is a critical design idea.

  • Notes = structured knowledge
  • Cards = memory tests

Anki encourages:

  • Reusing one note
  • Generating multiple cards
  • Testing knowledge from different angles

Why?

Because memory is context-dependent.

Knowing:

“TCP is connection-oriented”

Is different from answering:

  • “Which protocol is connection-oriented?”
  • “Is TCP connectionless?”
  • “Fill in the blank…”

docs.title: 7. Anki Separates Learning from Remembering
docs.text:
Most people mix these up.

Anki philosophy:

  • Learning happens outside
  • Remembering happens inside Anki

So Anki:

  • Does not explain concepts well
  • Does not teach from scratch
  • Assumes prior understanding

If you try to learn inside Anki:

  • Cards get bloated
  • Reviews become painful
  • Retention drops

Anki is a memory gym, not a classroom.

docs.title: 8. Consistency Beats Motivation
docs.text:
Anki is designed for:

  • Low daily effort
  • High long-term payoff

That’s why:

  • Reviews accumulate if skipped
  • There is no “pause learning” button
  • Anki feels unforgiving

This is intentional.

Anki’s belief:

A system that tolerates skipping will be abandoned.

docs.title: 9. Personal Truth > Objective Difficulty
docs.text:
Anki does not care if a card is “objectively easy”.

It cares:

  • How you answered
  • How you performed
  • How you forget

Two users with the same deck will get:

  • Different intervals
  • Different schedules
  • Different experiences

Anki adapts to your memory, not the content.

docs.title: 10. Automation Over Willpower
docs.text:
Anki removes human decision-making:

  • When to review
  • What to review
  • How often

Why?

Because willpower is unreliable.

Once a card exists:

  • You don’t negotiate with it
  • You just answer it

Anki replaces:

“Should I review this today?”

with

“Answer now.”

docs.title: 11. Pain Is a Signal
docs.text:
When Anki feels bad, it usually means:

  • Cards are too large
  • Too many new cards
  • Reviews were skipped
  • Poor card design

Anki’s discomfort is diagnostic.

Good Anki feels:

  • Slightly challenging
  • Fast-paced
  • Predictable

docs.title: 12. The Ultimate Design Principle
docs.text:
Anki is honest.

It shows you:

  • What you actually remember
  • What you are forgetting
  • The cost of skipping days

It does not flatter you.

It does not motivate you.

It does not lie.

And that honesty is why it works.

docs.title: Final Mental Model
docs.text:
Anki is a scheduler for forgetting.

If you design cards that respect:

  • Atomic knowledge
  • Active recall
  • Time efficiency

Anki will take care of the rest.

docs.title: Anki: Notes & Cards
docs.text:
How Anki Stores Knowledge vs How It Tests Memory

If you understand this chapter, you understand Anki.

docs.title: 1. The Core Distinction (Memorize This)
docs.text:
Notes store information.

Cards test memory.

You create notes.

Anki generates cards.

This separation is not cosmetic — it is a design principle.

docs.title: 2. What Is a Note?
docs.text:
A note is a structured container of information.

It is:

  • One concept
  • With multiple fields
  • Saved once

Examples of fields:

  • Term
  • Definition
  • Example
  • Explanation
  • Image
  • Extra info

A note is not something you review directly.

docs.title: 2.1 Example: Vocabulary Note
docs.text:
Fields:

Word: abandon
Meaning: give up completely
Example: He abandoned the plan.
Pronunciation: /əˈbændən/

This is one note.

docs.title: 3. What Is a Card?
docs.text:
A card is a question–answer pair generated from a note.

A card:

  • Has a front (question)
  • Has a back (answer)
  • Is scheduled for review
  • Is shown repeatedly over time

Cards are what Anki actually shows you.

docs.title: 3.1 Cards Generated from One Note
docs.text:
From the same vocabulary note, Anki can generate:

  • Card 1 Front: abandon Back: give up completely
  • Card 2 Front: give up completely Back: abandon
  • Card 3 Front: He ___ the plan. Back: abandoned

One note → multiple cards.

docs.title: 4. Why Anki Separates Notes and Cards
docs.text:
This separation allows:

  1. Reuse
    • One fact, many tests
  2. Consistency
    • Fix the note → all cards update
  3. Multiple recall directions
    • Recognition
    • Production
    • Contextual recall
  4. Better memory coverage
    • Memory is context-dependent

Anki tests how you know something, not just that you know it.

docs.title: 5. Note Types: The Blueprint
docs.text:
A note type defines:

  • What fields exist
  • How many cards are created
  • What each card looks like

Examples:

  • Basic
  • Basic (and reverse)
  • Cloze
  • Custom note types

Think of a note type as a card factory.

docs.title: 5.1 Basic Note Type
docs.text:
Fields:

Front
Back

Cards:

  • One card per note

Use when:

  • Knowledge is one-directional
  • You want simplicity

docs.title: 5.2 Basic (and Reverse)
docs.text:
Fields:

Front
Back

Cards:

  • Front → Back
  • Back → Front

Use when:

  • Both directions matter
  • Vocabulary, definitions

Caution:

  • Not always appropriate (not all facts are symmetric)

docs.title: 5.3 Cloze Note Type
docs.text:
Fields:

Text
Extra

Example note:

TCP is a {{c1::connection-oriented}} protocol.

Cards:

  • One per cloze deletion

Why cloze is powerful:

  • Keeps context
  • Encourages atomic deletions
  • Fast to create

docs.title: 6. Fields: Design Matters
docs.text:
Fields are raw data, not cards.

Good field design:

  • Clear purpose per field
  • No mixing of unrelated info
  • Optional extra fields allowed

Bad field design:

  • Huge paragraphs
  • Multiple concepts in one field
  • Formatting chaos

Rule:

If you hesitate while recalling, the card is poorly designed.

docs.title: 7. Card Templates: How Notes Become Cards
docs.text:
A card template decides:

  • What appears on the front
  • What appears on the back
  • How fields are arranged

Example template logic:

Front: {{Word}}
Back: {{Meaning}}<br>{{Example}}

Change the template:

  • All existing cards update
  • No need to re-enter notes

This is why notes are more important than cards.

docs.title: 8. One Note, Many Cards — But Not Too Many
docs.text:
Anki allows many cards per note, but:

Too few cards:

  • Poor coverage

Too many cards:

  • Review overload
  • Redundancy
  • Fatigue

Rule of thumb:

  • 1–5 cards per note
  • Each card tests a different angle

docs.title: Edit the note when:
docs.text:
• Content is wrong
  • Explanation is unclear
  • Example is bad

docs.title: Edit the card when:
docs.text:
• Question is poorly phrased
  • Front reveals the answer
  • Card is ambiguous

Most of the time:

Edit the note, not the card.

docs.title: “Why did editing one card change others?”
docs.text: Because they share the same note.

docs.title: “Why do I see cards I didn’t create?”
docs.text: Anki generated them from the note type.

docs.title: “Why does deleting a note delete many cards?”
docs.text: Because cards depend on the note.

docs.title: 11. Designing Notes with Memory in Mind
docs.text:
Ask while creating a note:

  • What might I forget?
  • In what direction will I need recall?
  • What context helps recall but doesn’t give away the answer?

Design notes so cards can be:

  • Short
  • Clear
  • Atomic

docs.title: 12. Mental Model to Keep Forever
docs.text:
Notes are knowledge.

Cards are questions.

Templates are factories.

If Anki feels hard:

  • Fix cards → short term
  • Fix notes → long term

docs.title: Final Advice
docs.text:
Most Anki problems are note design problems disguised as scheduling issues.

If you master notes and cards:

  • Reviews become fast
  • Retention becomes high
  • Anki becomes boring — in a good way

docs.title: Anki: Backup
docs.text:
What Is Backed Up, How, and How to Recover

If Anki matters to you, backups are not optional.

docs.title: 1. Why Backups Matter in Anki (More Than You Think)
docs.text:
Anki decks represent:

  • Thousands of hours of thinking
  • Carefully designed notes
  • Personalized scheduling history

Losing an Anki collection means:

  • Losing intervals
  • Losing learning progress
  • Losing the state of your memory

Anki backups protect far more than card text.

docs.title: 2. What Exactly Needs to Be Backed Up
docs.text: Anki data consists of three layers:

docs.title: 2.1 Content
docs.text:
• Notes
  • Fields
  • Tags
  • Deck structure

docs.title: 2.2 Scheduling State
docs.text:
• Review history
  • Intervals
  • Ease factors
  • Due dates

docs.title: 2.3 Media
docs.text:
• Images
  • Audio
  • Screenshots
  • Diagrams

A good backup strategy covers all three.

docs.title: 3.1 How Auto Backups Work
docs.text:
Every time you:

  • Open Anki
  • Close Anki
  • Sync

Anki silently creates a backup of:

  • Your entire collection database

These are stored locally.

docs.title: 3.2 What Is Included
docs.text:
Included:

  • All decks
  • All notes
  • All scheduling data

Not included:

  • Media files (images/audio)

This distinction is critical.

docs.title: 3.3 Where Auto Backups Are Stored
docs.text:
Typical locations:

  • macOS ~/Library/Application Support/Anki2/<Profile>/backups/
  • Windows %APPDATA%\Anki2\<Profile>\backups\
  • Linux ~/.local/share/Anki2/<Profile>/backups/

Files look like:

collection-2026-02-08-09-30.colpkg

They are timestamped snapshots.

docs.title: 3.4 How Many Backups Are Kept
docs.text:
Default:

  • Last 50 backups

Oldest backups are deleted automatically.

You can change this in:

Preferences → Backups

docs.title: 4.1 When to Restore
docs.text:
Common cases:

  • Accidental mass deletion
  • Bad add-on behavior
  • Sync conflict resolution mistake
  • Corrupted collection

docs.title: 4.2 Restore Process (Desktop)
docs.text:
1. Open Anki
  2. File → Switch Profile
  3. Click Open Backup
  4. Choose a backup by timestamp
  5. Confirm restore

This replaces your current collection.

⚠️ Restore before syncing again.

docs.title: 5. AnkiWeb Sync Is NOT a Backup
docs.text: This is a very common misconception.

docs.title: 5.1 What Sync Does
docs.text:
• Keeps devices consistent
  • Mirrors changes everywhere

docs.title: 5.2 What Sync Does NOT Do
docs.text:
• No version history
  • No undo
  • No protection from mistakes

If you delete something and sync:

  • It is deleted everywhere

👉 Sync = replication, not backup.

docs.title: 6.1 Why Manual Exports Matter
docs.text:
Manual exports:

  • Include media files
  • Are portable
  • Can be stored offline

Use them as milestones:

  • Monthly
  • Before major edits
  • Before add-on experiments

docs.title: 6.2 How to Export Properly
docs.text:
1. Select All Decks
  2. File → Export
  3. Choose:
    • Format: Anki Deck Package (*.apkg)
    • ✔️ Include media
    • ✔️ Include scheduling information

This creates a self-contained archive.

docs.title: 6.3 What an .apkg Contains
docs.text:
• All notes
  • All cards
  • Scheduling state
  • All media files

This is the gold standard backup.

docs.title: 7. Media Folder Backup (Often Forgotten)
docs.text:
Media files live separately from the database.

Folder:

collection.media/

Problems if not backed up:

  • Missing images
  • Broken audio
  • Blank cards

Best practice:

  • Back up the entire Anki2 folder, not just files inside it.

docs.title: 8. Profiles and Backups
docs.text:
Each profile has:

  • Separate collection
  • Separate backups
  • Separate media

If you use multiple profiles:

  • Back them all up
  • Restore carefully to the correct profile

docs.title: 9.1 The 3-Layer Model
docs.text:
1. Anki auto backups (short-term safety)
  2. Manual .apkg exports (medium-term safety)
  3. System-level backups (long-term safety)

Examples:

  • Time Machine (macOS)
  • Cloud storage
  • External disk

docs.title: 9.2 When to Create Manual Backups
docs.text:
Always do it before:

  • Installing new add-ons
  • Bulk editing notes
  • Changing note types
  • Importing large decks

docs.title: Scenario 1: Accidental Deletion
docs.text: → Restore from auto backup

docs.title: Scenario 2: Broken Media
docs.text: → Restore collection.media from system backup

docs.title: Scenario 3: Sync Conflict Gone Wrong
docs.text: → Restore backup, then force upload

docs.title: Scenario 4: Add-on Corruption
docs.text: → Restore backup made before installation

docs.title: 11. Things Backups Cannot Save You From
docs.text:
• Poor card design
  • Overloaded decks
  • Burnout from too many reviews

Backups protect data — not decisions.

docs.title: 12. Golden Rules to Remember
docs.text:
1. Sync is not backup
  2. Auto backups don’t include media
  3. Manual exports are your lifeline
  4. Never sync after a mistake before restoring
  5. Back up before experimenting

docs.title: Final Mental Model
docs.text:
Anki backups preserve not just information, but time.

Your decks represent:

  • Past effort
  • Future efficiency

Protect them like source code.

docs.title: 1. What EndNote actually is (and what it is not)
docs.text:
EndNote is a reference manager, not a PDF reader and not a word processor.

Its core jobs are:

  • Store bibliographic records (author, title, journal, year, DOI, etc.)
  • Attach and manage PDF files
  • Insert citations into Word
  • Automatically generate reference lists in a required style (APA, IEEE, Chicago…)

Think of EndNote as a database + file manager for academic papers.

docs.title: 2. Mental model: how EndNote stores things on disk
docs.text: This part is critical and often misunderstood.

docs.title: An EndNote “library” is NOT a single file
docs.text:
When you create a library called:

MyResearch.enl

EndNote actually creates two things in the filesystem:

MyResearch.enl
MyResearch.Data/

docs.title: What each part does
docs.text:
Item Purpose MyResearch.enl The database index (metadata, links, notes) MyResearch.Data/ All attachments, PDFs, figures, cache files

💡 Rule #1:

The .enl file and .Data folder must always stay together.

If you move, rename, or delete only one of them, the library breaks.

docs.title: 3. Where you should store your EndNote library
Best practice locations
docs.text:
• A dedicated folder like:

    Documents/
  EndNote/
    MyResearch.enl
    MyResearch.Data/

  • Or a synced folder only if syncing is safe (more on this later)

docs.title: Locations to avoid
docs.text:
❌ Desktop (easy to accidentally delete)

❌ Temporary folders

❌ USB drives (unless read-only use)

❌ Directly inside cloud-sync folders (Dropbox, iCloud) without precautions

docs.title: Option A: PDFs attached to references (recommended)
docs.text:
When you:

  • Import a paper
  • Or drag a PDF into EndNote

EndNote will:

  1. Copy the PDF

  2. Store it inside:

    MyResearch.Data/PDF/

  3. Link it to the reference record

You do not need to remember where the PDF is stored.

docs.title: Option B: Linking to external PDFs (advanced, not recommended for beginners)
docs.text:
EndNote can link to PDFs stored elsewhere, but:

  • Moving the file breaks the link
  • Cloud syncing becomes risky

For beginners: don’t do this.

docs.title: 5. Automatic PDF organization (very important setting)
docs.text:
Go to:

EndNote → Settings → PDF Handling

Enable:

  • ✅ Automatically rename PDF files
  • ✅ Automatically import PDFs

Typical rename format:

Author + Year + Title.pdf

Example:

Smith_2022_Neural_Networks.pdf

This gives you:

  • Clean filenames
  • Consistent organization
  • Easier recovery if something breaks

docs.title: Method 1: Direct export from databases
docs.text:
From sources like:

  • Google Scholar
  • Web of Science
  • PubMed
  • IEEE Xplore

You usually download a file like:

citation.enw

When opened:

  • EndNote reads metadata
  • Creates a new record
  • Optionally downloads PDFs

Filesystem-wise:

  • Metadata goes into .enl
  • PDFs go into .Data/PDF/

docs.title: Method 2: Drag & drop PDFs
docs.text:
You can drag a PDF into EndNote.

EndNote will:

  1. Try to extract metadata (title, author, DOI)
  2. Create a reference automatically

If metadata fails:

  • You can edit it manually later

docs.title: Groups are NOT filesystem folders
docs.text:
In EndNote:

  • Groups are like tags or playlists
  • A reference can appear in multiple groups
  • Deleting a group does not delete the reference

On disk:

  • Nothing changes
  • Files remain in .Data/

Think:

Groups = logical organization

Filesystem = physical storage

docs.title: The correct way to back up an EndNote library
docs.text:
Use:

File → Compressed Library (.enlx)...

This creates one file:

MyResearch.enlx

Which contains:

  • .enl
  • .Data/
  • All PDFs

This is the only safe way to:

  • Move libraries
  • Send them to others
  • Store backups

docs.title: Backup frequency
docs.text:
• Weekly minimum
  • Before major edits
  • Before OS upgrades

docs.title: The danger
docs.text:
Cloud tools:

  • Sync file-by-file
  • EndNote expects atomic database operations

This can cause:

  • Corrupted libraries
  • Missing PDFs
  • Broken indexes

docs.title: Safe approaches
docs.text:
✅ Best:

  • Store library locally
  • Sync only .enlx backups

✅ Acceptable (advanced users):

  • Use EndNote Online sync
  • Or ensure EndNote is closed before cloud sync

❌ Unsafe:

  • Actively opening .enl inside a syncing folder

docs.title: 10. Using EndNote with Word
docs.text:
When you insert citations:

  • EndNote does not copy PDFs into Word
  • Word stores citation placeholders
  • Formatting happens dynamically

Your Word file depends on:

  • The EndNote library being available
  • Matching record IDs

💡 If you send a Word file to someone:

  • Also send the .enlx library

docs.title: 11. Common beginner mistakes (and how to avoid them)
docs.text: Mistake Fix Moving only .enl Always move .enl + .Data Storing library on Desktop Use Documents folder Cloud sync corruption Use .enlx backups Renaming PDFs manually Let EndNote manage PDFs Using Finder/Explorer to clean files Never touch .Data manually

docs.title: 12. A simple, recommended workflow
docs.text:
1. Create one main library per project
  2. Store it locally
  3. Import references from databases
  4. Let EndNote manage PDFs
  5. Organize with Groups
  6. Back up weekly as .enlx
  7. Insert citations only via Word plugin

docs.title: 13. Final takeaway
docs.text:
If you remember only three things, remember these:

  1. .enl and .Data are inseparable
  2. Never manually edit EndNote’s internal folders
  3. Backups should be .enlx, not raw files

docs.title: 0. Core Principle (Read This First)
docs.text:
EndNote libraries are databases, not documents.

That means:

  • You must back up the entire library structure
  • You must avoid syncing live libraries improperly
  • You should separate “working copies” and “archive backups”

docs.title: 1.1 .enl Is Only the Tip of the Iceberg
docs.text:
A normal EndNote library looks like this:

MyLibrary.enl
MyLibrary.Data/
├── PDF/
├── rdb/
├── tdb/
├── sdb/
├── Figures/
└── trash/

Critical rule

⚠️ Backing up only MyLibrary.enl = guaranteed data loss

You must back up:

  • MyLibrary.enl
  • MyLibrary.Data/ (entire folder)

Treat them as atomic.

docs.title: 1.2 Compressed Library = Safe Atomic Unit
docs.text:
EndNote’s safest backup format:

MyLibrary.enlx

This is:

  • A single file
  • Internally consistent
  • Ideal for archives, cloud storage, and versioning

Advanced rule:

.enlx is for backup & transfer, not daily editing.

docs.title: 2.1 The 3-2-1 Rule (Still Gold Standard)
docs.text:
For EndNote, interpret it like this:

Rule EndNote Implementation 3 copies Working library + local backup + off-site 2 media Local disk + cloud / NAS 1 off-site Cloud or physical external drive

docs.title: 2.2 Split Your Backups by Purpose
docs.text: Type Format Frequency Editable Working library .enl + .Data Daily ✅ Snapshot backup .enlx Daily / Weekly ❌ Archive backup .enlx Monthly / Milestone ❌ Export safety net .xml / .ris Monthly ❌

docs.title: 3.1 Versioned Snapshot Backups (Highly Recommended)
docs.text:
Use date-stamped .enlx files:

EndNote_Backups/
├── MyLibrary_2026-02-01.enlx
├── MyLibrary_2026-02-05.enlx
├── MyLibrary_2026-02-10.enlx

Why this matters

  • Protects against silent corruption
  • Lets you roll back weeks or months
  • Works even if EndNote itself breaks

docs.title: 3.2 Automate Local Backups (macOS example)
docs.text:
Workflow

  1. Close EndNote
  2. Create compressed library
  3. Move to backup folder
  4. Sync elsewhere

On macOS, pair EndNote with:

  • Shortcuts
  • Hazel
  • Keyboard Maestro
  • launchd

Key rule

Never compress a library while EndNote is open.

docs.title: 4. Cloud Sync: What’s Safe, What’s Dangerous
4.1 EndNote Sync ≠ Backup
docs.text:
EndNote’s built-in sync:

  • Syncs references
  • Syncs PDFs
  • ❌ Does not protect against accidental deletion or corruption

Use it for convenience, not recovery.

docs.title: 4.2 Cloud Services: The Correct Way
docs.text:
Service Safe Method iCloud / Dropbox / OneDrive Sync only .enlx backups NAS (Time Machine, rsync) Full library OK Git ❌ Not recommended for .enl

Never

  • Edit a live .enl inside a cloud-synced folder
  • Open the same library on two machines simultaneously

docs.title: 5. Time Machine / NAS / rsync (Power User Tier)
5.1 Time Machine (macOS)
docs.text:
Pros:

  • Automatic
  • Versioned
  • Recovers individual PDFs

Cons:

  • Can back up corruption if EndNote was open

Rule

Always close EndNote before major edits

docs.title: 5.2 rsync Snapshot Strategy (Advanced)
docs.text:
Example logic:

rsync -a --delete \
~/EndNote/ \
/Volumes/NAS/EndNote_Backups/

Combine with:

  • ZFS / Btrfs snapshots
  • NAS versioning

This gives enterprise-grade recovery.

docs.title: 6.1 XML Export (EndNote Native)
docs.text:
Export:

  • EndNote XML
  • Include: references + PDFs + groups

Pros:

  • Best metadata preservation
  • Cross-version compatible

docs.title: 6.2 RIS / BibTeX (Interoperability)
docs.text:
Use for:

  • Migration safety
  • Long-term archival
  • Future software compatibility

Rule

These are backups of content, not structure.

docs.title: Scenario A: Library Won’t Open
docs.text:
1. Restore latest .enlx
  2. Extract to local disk
  3. Open extracted .enl

docs.title: Scenario B: Sync Deleted References
docs.text:
1. Disconnect sync immediately
  2. Restore older .enlx
  3. Compare & re-import

docs.title: Scenario C: PDF Folder Corrupted
docs.text:
1. Restore from Time Machine / NAS
  2. Replace MyLibrary.Data/PDF/

docs.title: 8. Common Advanced Mistakes (Avoid These)
docs.text:
❌ Relying only on EndNote Sync

❌ Syncing live libraries via Dropbox

❌ Backing up while EndNote is open

❌ Keeping only one backup

❌ No date/version in backup names

docs.title: 9. Recommended “Gold Standard” Setup
docs.text:
Ideal advanced setup

  • Daily .enlx snapshots (local)
  • Time Machine (hourly)
  • Weekly cloud-synced .enlx
  • Monthly XML export

If your EndNote library disappeared tomorrow, you’d lose at most 24 hours — and probably nothing.

docs.title: 10. Final Advice (From Hard-Won Experience)
docs.text:
If it’s not versioned, it’s not a backup.

If it’s not offline somewhere, it’s not safe.

If you can’t restore it, it doesn’t exist.

docs.title: 1. What Is a Reference Type?
docs.text:
In EndNote, a Reference Type defines:

  • What kind of source a reference is (book, journal article, thesis, etc.)
  • Which fields are available for that source
  • How those fields are interpreted by citation styles

💡 In short:

Reference Type = “Template” that tells EndNote how to store and format a reference

Examples:

  • Journal Article → has Journal, Volume, Issue
  • Book → has Publisher, Place Published
  • Thesis → has Degree, University

docs.title: 2. Why Reference Type Matters (Very Important)
docs.text: Choosing the correct reference type affects:

docs.title: ① Citation Formatting Accuracy
docs.text:
• APA, MLA, Chicago, Vancouver, etc. depend on reference type
  • Wrong type = missing or misplaced elements

docs.title: ② Field Availability
docs.text:
• Fields differ by reference type
  • Example:
    • Book → Publisher
    • Journal Article → Journal
    • Web Page → URL, Access Date

docs.title: ③ Export & Compatibility
docs.text: • Bibliographies exported to Word, LaTeX, or other tools rely on reference type

docs.title: 3. Core Reference Types You Must Know
3.1 Journal Article (Most Common)
docs.text:
Use when: The source is published in a scholarly journal.

Key fields

  • Author
  • Year
  • Title
  • Journal
  • Volume
  • Issue
  • Pages
  • DOI

Correct example

Author: Smith, John
Year: 2022
Title: Language acquisition in adults
Journal: Applied Linguistics
Volume: 43
Issue: 2
Pages: 210–230
DOI: 10.xxxx/xxxx

❌ Do NOT use for:

  • Conference proceedings
  • Magazine articles (unless academic)

docs.title: 3.2 Book
docs.text:
Use when: A whole book written by one or more authors.

Key fields

  • Author
  • Year
  • Title
  • Publisher
  • Place Published
  • Edition

📌 For translated books:

  • Use Translated Title for the translated name
  • Original title often goes in:
    • Original Title (if available), or
    • Title (original) + Translated Title

docs.title: 3.3 Book Section (Book Chapter)
docs.text:
Use when: One chapter in an edited book.

Key fields

  • Author (chapter author)
  • Year
  • Title (chapter title)
  • Editor
  • Book Title
  • Pages
  • Publisher

⚠️ Common mistake:

❌ Using Book instead of Book Section

docs.title: 3.4 Conference Paper / Proceedings
docs.text:
Conference Paper

  • Individual paper presented at a conference

Conference Proceedings

  • Whole published proceedings volume

Key fields

  • Author
  • Year
  • Title
  • Conference Name
  • Place Published
  • Publisher

docs.title: 3.5 Thesis / Dissertation
docs.text:
Use when: Academic degree work.

Key fields

  • Author
  • Year
  • Title
  • Degree
  • University
  • Place Published

Example:

Degree: PhD dissertation
University: University of Cambridge

docs.title: 3.6 Web Page
docs.text:
Use when: Online-only sources without formal publication structure.

Key fields

  • Author / Corporate Author
  • Year
  • Title
  • URL
  • Access Date

⚠️ Use sparingly for academic writing if a better type exists.

docs.title: 3.7 Report
docs.text:
Use when: Institutional or government publications.

Key fields

  • Author / Institution
  • Year
  • Title
  • Report Number
  • Publisher
  • URL (optional)

Examples:

  • OECD reports
  • Government white papers

docs.title: 4. Less Common but Useful Reference Types
docs.text: Reference Type Use Case Magazine Article Popular magazines Newspaper Article Newspapers Preprint arXiv / bioRxiv Dataset Research data Software Software tools Patent Patent documents Manuscript Unpublished work Map Cartographic material Audiovisual Material Videos, films

docs.title: 5. How EndNote Chooses Fields (Behind the Scenes)
docs.text:
• Each reference type has a fixed field structure
  • Citation styles decide:
    • which fields are used
    • in what order
    • with what punctuation

Example:

  • APA style:
    • Uses DOI for Journal Article
    • Ignores URL if DOI exists

docs.title: 6. Custom Reference Types (Advanced)
docs.text: You can customize reference types, but with caution.

docs.title: Where to configure:
docs.text:
EndNote → Settings / Preferences → Reference Types

You can:

  • Rename reference types
  • Enable / disable types
  • Add custom fields

⚠️ Best practice

  • Do NOT heavily customize if:
    • You sync across devices
    • You collaborate with others
    • You submit manuscripts to journals

docs.title: 7. Choosing the Right Reference Type (Decision Guide)
docs.text: Source Correct Type Journal PDF Journal Article Book (whole) Book Chapter in edited book Book Section arXiv paper Preprint Government PDF Report Blog post Web Page Master’s / PhD work Thesis Conference presentation Conference Paper

docs.title: 8. Common Mistakes (Very Common)
docs.text:
❌ Using Journal Article for everything

❌ Putting journal name in Publisher

❌ Using Web Page for published PDFs

❌ Mixing Book and Book Section

❌ Ignoring DOI field

docs.title: 9. Expert Best Practices
docs.text:
✔ Always choose the most specific reference type

✔ Fill all relevant fields, not just the minimum

✔ Keep one consistent rule for translated works

✔ Use DOI whenever available

✔ Fix reference type before writing the paper

docs.title: 10. Final Mental Model
docs.text:
Reference Type = Structure

Fields = Data

Citation Style = Presentation

docs.title: EndNote: Book
docs.text: Book Reference Type (with a Focus on Chinese Books)

docs.title: 1. What is “Book” in EndNote?
docs.text:
The Book reference type is used for:

  • 📘 Monographs / 专著
  • 📚 Single-volume books
  • 📕 Translated books (中译本 / 外文译本)

Do NOT use Book for:

  • Chapters in edited books → use Book Section

docs.title: 1️⃣ What Is 2FA?
docs.text:
2FA (Two-Factor Authentication) is an extra layer of security added to your password.

Normally, you log in with:

✅ Something you know → your password

With 2FA, you must also provide:

✅ Something you have (like your phone)

or

✅ Something you are (like your fingerprint)

So even if someone steals your password, they still can’t log in without the second factor.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Why 2FA Is Important
docs.text:
Passwords alone are not enough because they can be:

  • Guessed
  • Reused across sites
  • Leaked in data breaches
  • Phished through fake websites

For example, if your account on Facebook or Google gets compromised, attackers may gain access to:

  • Your private messages
  • Your email
  • Password reset links
  • Financial data

2FA dramatically reduces this risk.

Even if your password leaks, your account stays protected.

docs.title: 3️⃣ The Three Authentication Factors
docs.text: Security experts divide authentication into three types:

docs.title: 1️⃣ Something You Know
docs.text:
• Password
  • PIN

docs.title: 2️⃣ Something You Have
docs.text:
• Phone
  • Hardware key
  • Authentication app

docs.title: 3️⃣ Something You Are
docs.text:
• Fingerprint
  • Face recognition

2FA simply means using two different categories together.

docs.title: 4️⃣ Common Types of 2FA (From Weakest to Strongest)
📱 1. SMS Codes (Basic Level)
docs.text:
You receive a 6-digit code via text message.

Example:

  • You enter your password.
  • A code is sent to your phone.
  • You enter the code to log in.

✔ Easy to use

❌ Vulnerable to SIM swapping attacks

Better than nothing, but not the best option.

docs.title: 📲 2. Authenticator Apps (Recommended)
docs.text:
Apps generate a new 6-digit code every 30 seconds.

Popular apps include:

  • Google Authenticator
  • Microsoft Authenticator
  • Authy

How it works:

  • You scan a QR code when enabling 2FA.
  • The app generates time-based codes (TOTP).
  • You enter the current code when logging in.

✔ Works offline

✔ More secure than SMS

✔ Widely supported

For most beginners, this is the best choice.

docs.title: 🔑 3. Hardware Security Keys (Most Secure)
docs.text:
Physical devices you plug in or tap.

Examples:

  • YubiKey

How it works:

  • Insert or tap the key
  • Press a button to confirm

✔ Extremely secure

✔ Resistant to phishing

✔ Used by security professionals

This is ideal for:

  • Journalists
  • Developers
  • Business accounts
  • Anyone serious about security

docs.title: 5️⃣ What Is TOTP?
docs.text:
Most authenticator apps use:

TOTP = Time-Based One-Time Password

  • Code changes every 30 seconds
  • Based on a shared secret
  • Works without internet

It’s secure because attackers cannot reuse old codes.

docs.title: 6️⃣ How to Enable 2FA (General Steps)
docs.text:
Although every website is slightly different, the process is usually:

  1. Go to Account Settings
  2. Open Security
  3. Click Enable Two-Factor Authentication
  4. Choose:
    • SMS, or
    • Authenticator app (recommended)
  5. Save your backup codes

docs.title: 7️⃣ VERY IMPORTANT: Backup Codes
docs.text:
When enabling 2FA, websites give you:

🔐 Backup recovery codes

These are one-time emergency codes in case you lose your phone.

You should:

  • Save them in a password manager
  • Print them and store safely
  • Never screenshot and forget them

If you lose both your password and 2FA device without backups, account recovery can be very difficult.

docs.title: 8️⃣ Common Beginner Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Only enabling SMS 2FA

❌ Not saving backup codes

❌ Not backing up authenticator apps

❌ Storing recovery codes in email

docs.title: 9️⃣ Should You Use 2FA Everywhere?
docs.text:
Priority accounts:

  • Email (most important!)
  • Password manager
  • Banking
  • Cloud storage
  • Social media

If your email is hacked, attackers can reset everything else.

docs.title: 🔟 2FA vs MFA
docs.text:
You may also hear:

MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication)

MFA = two or more factors

2FA = exactly two factors

In daily conversation, people use them interchangeably.

docs.title: Final Advice for Beginners
docs.text:
If you do only one thing after reading this guide:

Enable authenticator-app-based 2FA on your email account today.

It is one of the highest security improvements you can make with minimal effort.

docs.title: 1. The problem E2EE is trying to solve
docs.text:
Imagine you send a postcard 📮:

  • Anyone handling it (post office, delivery staff) can read the content
  • You trust them not to, but technically they can

Now imagine sending a locked box 🔒:

  • Only you and the receiver have the keys
  • Everyone in between can see the box, but cannot open it

👉 End-to-End Encryption = sending locked boxes instead of postcards

docs.title: 2. What “End-to-End” actually means
docs.text:
“End” = the sender’s device

“End” = the receiver’s device

Encryption happens:

  • 🔐 on your device before sending
  • 🔓 on the recipient’s device after receiving

Important consequence:

  • ❌ Server providers cannot read your data
  • ❌ Hackers breaking into servers get only ciphertext
  • ❌ Even the company running the service cannot decrypt your messages

Examples of E2EE services:

  • Signal
  • WhatsApp (messages)
  • iMessage
  • Proton Mail (between Proton users)

docs.title: 🔓 Transport encryption (TLS / HTTPS)
docs.text:
Most websites use this.

  • Data is encrypted between you and the server
  • The server can decrypt and read your data

Think:

“Encrypted tunnel, but the server sees everything”

docs.title: 🔐 End-to-End encryption
docs.text:
• Data is encrypted from sender to receiver
  • The server never has the keys

Think:

“The server is just a mailman carrying locked boxes”

docs.title: 4. The two types of keys (no math, promise)
🔑 Symmetric encryption (one key)
docs.text:
• Same key encrypts and decrypts
  • Fast, efficient
  • Problem: how do you share the key safely?

Analogy:

  • One shared password
  • Anyone who knows it can open the box

docs.title: 🔑 Asymmetric encryption (key pairs)
docs.text:
This is the magic that makes E2EE possible ✨

Each user has:

  • Public key → can be shared
  • Private key → never shared, stays on device

What they do:

  • Public key 🔓 locks the message
  • Private key 🔐 unlocks it

Analogy:

  • Public key = mailbox slot
  • Private key = mailbox key

Anyone can drop mail in, only you can open it.

docs.title: 5. How E2EE works step-by-step (simple version)
docs.text: Let’s say Alice sends a message to Bob.

docs.title: Step 1: Key exchange
docs.text:
• Bob creates a key pair
  • Bob shares his public key
  • Bob keeps his private key secret

docs.title: Step 2: Encrypt on sender’s device
docs.text:
• Alice uses Bob’s public key to encrypt the message
  • Message becomes unreadable ciphertext

docs.title: Step 3: Server delivery
docs.text:
• Server receives encrypted data
  • Server stores or forwards it
  • Server cannot decrypt it

docs.title: Step 4: Decrypt on receiver’s device
docs.text:
• Bob uses his private key
  • Message becomes readable again

✔ Only Bob can read it

✔ Even the service provider cannot

docs.title: ✅ Advantages
docs.text:
• Strong privacy
  • Protection against data breaches
  • Protection from mass surveillance
  • Trust minimized (you don’t need to trust the company)

docs.title: ⚠️ Limitations
docs.text:
• Lose your private key → data is gone forever
  • Harder to recover accounts
  • Law enforcement can’t “just ask the company”
  • Metadata (who talked to whom, when) may still exist

docs.title: 7. What E2EE does not protect against
docs.text:
Very important reality check 🚨

E2EE does NOT protect you if:

  • Your device is compromised (malware, spyware)
  • You share your private keys or passwords
  • You back up data unencrypted to the cloud
  • Someone physically accesses your unlocked device

👉 Encryption protects data in transit and storage, not bad device security

docs.title: 8. E2EE and backups (common beginner mistake)
docs.text:
Many apps:

  • Encrypt messages
  • BUT back them up unencrypted to cloud services

Example:

  • WhatsApp without encrypted backups
  • Messaging apps syncing plaintext backups to iCloud / Google Drive

Best practice:

  • Use end-to-end encrypted backups
  • Or manage your own encrypted backup system

docs.title: 9. Real-world analogy summary
docs.text: Concept Analogy Plaintext Open postcard Encryption Locked box Public key Mail slot Private key Mailbox key Server Mail carrier E2EE Only sender & receiver have keys

docs.title: 10. When you should care about E2EE
docs.text:
You don’t need to be a spy 🕵️

E2EE matters if you care about:

  • Private conversations
  • Business or academic work
  • Passwords & credentials
  • Personal photos & files
  • Freedom from data mining

docs.title: 11. One-sentence takeaway
docs.text: End-to-end encryption means your data is encrypted on your device, decrypted only on the recipient’s device, and unreadable to everyone in between — including the service provider.

docs.title: 1. What is a passkey?
docs.text:
A passkey is a new way to sign in without typing a password.

Instead of remembering something (a password), you prove it’s you using:

  • Face ID / Touch ID
  • Windows Hello
  • Your device PIN
  • Or a hardware security key

In practice:

You tap “Sign in with passkey” → authenticate locally → you’re logged in.

No password to type. No password to steal.

docs.title: 2. Why do we even need passkeys?
docs.text: Passwords have… issues 😅

docs.title: Problems with passwords
docs.text:
• People reuse them
  • They get phished
  • They get leaked in breaches
  • Strong ones are hard to remember
  • Weak ones are easy to guess

docs.title: What passkeys fix
docs.text:
• Phishing-resistant (you can’t be tricked into typing one)
  • No reuse (each site gets its own)
  • Nothing to remember
  • Much harder to steal

This isn’t a random idea—passkeys are backed by:

  • Apple
  • Google
  • Microsoft
  • The FIDO (Fast IDentity Online) Alliance

So yeah, this is the real future.

docs.title: 3. How passkeys work (no math, I promise)
docs.text:
Under the hood, passkeys use public-key cryptography.

Here’s the simple version:

docs.title: When you create a passkey
docs.text:
1. Your device generates a key pair
    • 🔑 Private key → stays on your device
    • 🔓 Public key → sent to the website
  2. The website stores only the public key

docs.title: When you log in
docs.text:
1. The website sends a challenge
  2. Your device signs it with the private key
  3. The website verifies it using the public key
  4. You’re in 🎉

Important:

Your private key never leaves your device.

docs.title: 4. What a passkey looks like in real life
Creating a passkey
docs.text:
You might see:

  • “Create a passkey”
  • “Use Face ID / Touch ID”
  • “Save a passkey to your device”

You authenticate once, and that’s it.

docs.title: Logging in later
docs.text:
Instead of:

Username + Password + 2FA

You get:

Use passkey → Face ID → Logged in

Fast. Clean. Secure.

docs.title: 5. Where are passkeys stored?
docs.text:
Passkeys live in secure storage on your device.

Common examples:

  • Apple: iCloud Keychain
  • Google: Google Password Manager
  • Microsoft: Windows Hello
  • Password managers: 1Password, Bitwarden, etc.

If syncing is enabled:

  • Your passkeys are end-to-end encrypted
  • They follow you across devices

docs.title: 6. Are passkeys really more secure?
docs.text: Short answer: yes, by a lot.

docs.title: Passkeys vs passwords
docs.text:
Feature Passwords Passkeys Phishing resistant ❌ ✅ Reusable ❌ ✅ (unique per site) Stored on server ❌ (hash) ❌ (only public key) Needs 2FA Often Usually not Easy to use 😐 😄

Passkeys eliminate entire classes of attacks.

docs.title: 7. What if I lose my device?
docs.text: This is the #1 beginner worry—totally fair.

docs.title: What usually saves you
docs.text:
• Passkeys synced via iCloud / Google
  • Another trusted device
  • Account recovery methods
  • Backup codes (on some services)

docs.title: Best practice
docs.text:
• Use at least two devices
  • Enable cloud sync
  • Keep recovery options updated

Passkeys are safer than passwords—but account recovery still matters.

docs.title: 8. Do passkeys replace passwords completely?
docs.text: Not yet—but they’re getting close.

docs.title: Current reality
docs.text:
• Many sites support both
  • Some still fall back to passwords
  • Enterprise systems are slower to adopt

docs.title: Where passkeys already work well
docs.text:
• Google
  • Apple ID
  • Microsoft
  • GitHub
  • Many modern web services

Expect this to accelerate fast.

docs.title: 9. Should beginners use passkeys?
docs.text:
Honestly? Yes.

If you:

  • Hate remembering passwords
  • Want better security without effort
  • Already use Face ID / Touch ID

Then passkeys are basically a free upgrade.

docs.title: 10. Beginner tips (important)
docs.text:
• ✔ Enable passkeys where available
  • ✔ Keep devices updated
  • ✔ Turn on cloud sync
  • ✔ Don’t disable recovery options
  • ❌ Don’t rely on only one device

docs.title: Final takeaway
docs.text:
Passkeys are:

  • Safer than passwords
  • Easier than passwords
  • Designed for normal people

This is one of those rare tech changes where security and convenience both win.

docs.title: 1. What Is Bitwarden?
docs.text:
Bitwarden is an open-source, cross-platform password manager that helps you:

  • Store usernames, passwords, passkeys, and secure notes
  • Generate strong, unique passwords
  • Autofill login forms on websites and apps
  • Sync your vault across devices securely
  • Share passwords safely (with family or teams)

It uses end-to-end encryption, meaning only you can see your data — not even Bitwarden.

docs.title: 2. Why Use a Password Manager?
docs.text:
Without a password manager:

  • You reuse weak passwords 😬
  • You forget passwords
  • Password breaches affect multiple accounts

With Bitwarden:

  • One strong master password
  • All other passwords are unique & random
  • Much safer and more convenient ✅

docs.title: 3. Bitwarden Plans (Simple Overview)
docs.text:
Plan Cost For whom Free $0 Most individuals (recommended) Premium ~$10/year Extra security features Family / Teams Paid Sharing with others

👉 Free plan is enough for most beginners.

docs.title: 4. Creating Your Bitwarden Account
docs.text:

  2. Click Create Account
  3. Enter:

    • Master Password (very important)
  4. Create a Password Hint (optional but helpful)
  5. Submit

docs.title: 🔐 Master Password Rules
docs.text:
• Long (12–16+ characters)
  • Unique (never reuse)
  • Easy for you to remember, hard for others

Example pattern (don’t copy exactly):

Correct-Horse!Battery#2026

⚠️ Bitwarden cannot recover your master password if you forget it.

docs.title: 5. Install Bitwarden on Your Devices
docs.text: You can use Bitwarden on multiple platforms.

docs.title: 9. Generating Strong Passwords
docs.text:
Never create passwords yourself again.

  1. Click Password Generator
  2. Choose:
    • Length (14–20 recommended)
    • Letters + numbers + symbols
  3. Click Copy
  4. Use it when signing up

✅ Each site gets a unique password

docs.title: Folders

• Work
  • Personal
  • Banking
  • School

docs.title: Search

docs.title: 🔒 Two-Factor Authentication (Highly Recommended)

1. Vault → Settings → Security

  • Vault syncs automatically

docs.title: 15. Free vs Premium — Should You Upgrade?
docs.text:
Premium gives:

  • TOTP inside Bitwarden
  • Security reports
  • Emergency access

💡 Not required at the start, but worth it long-term.

docs.title: 16. Best Practices Summary
docs.text:

  • Enable 2FA
  • Generate passwords for every site
  • Lock your vault when not in use
  • Keep Bitwarden as the only password storage

docs.title: 17. Final Thoughts
docs.text:
Bitwarden is:

  • Secure 🔐

  • Beginner-friendly

⚠️ Important note

docs.title: 0. Why Vaultwarden Backups Matter (Reality Check)
docs.text:
Vaultwarden stores everything that matters in just a few places:

  • Your encrypted vault data
  • User accounts & orgs
  • Attachments
  • Keys & settings

If you lose these and don’t have a backup, recovery is impossible — encryption means no second chances.

Rule #1: Vaultwarden backups are more important than server backups.

docs.title: 1. What Exactly Needs to Be Backed Up
Core components (must-have)
docs.text: Component Why it matters db.sqlite3 Contains all vault metadata attachments/ File uploads (secure notes, files) rsa_key.* Server-side encryption keys config.json / env vars Required for restore consistency

docs.title: Typical Docker layout
docs.text:
/vaultwarden/
├── db.sqlite3
├── attachments/
├── rsa_key.pem
├── rsa_key.pub.pem
├── config.json

⚠️ If you lose rsa_key.pem, all data is permanently unreadable.

docs.title: Strategy A — Cold File Backup (Most Common)
docs.text:
• Stop container
  • Copy files
  • Restart container

Pros: safest

Cons: brief downtime

docs.title: Strategy B — Hot Backup (No Downtime)
docs.text:
• Copy files while running
  • SQLite-safe if done correctly

Pros: no service interruption

Cons: must be careful

docs.title: Strategy C — Logical Export (User-level)
docs.text:
• Bitwarden clients export vaults

Pros: portable

Cons: not a server backup

Best practice: A + B + periodic user exports

docs.title: Step 1: Ensure WAL mode (recommended)
docs.text:
Vaultwarden uses SQLite WAL by default. Confirm:

sqlite3 db.sqlite3 "PRAGMA journal_mode;"

Expected:

wal

docs.title: Step 2: Snapshot required files
docs.text:
tar -czf vaultwarden-backup-$(date +%F).tar.gz \
  db.sqlite3 \
  db.sqlite3-wal \
  db.sqlite3-shm \
  attachments/ \
  rsa_key.pem \
  rsa_key.pub.pem

✔ This produces a consistent backup.

docs.title: 4. Cold Backup (Safest Method)
docs.text:
docker stop vaultwarden

tar -czf vaultwarden-backup-$(date +%F).tar.gz \
  /path/to/vaultwarden/

docker start vaultwarden

Downtime: usually < 5 seconds

docs.title: Example volume mapping
docs.text:
volumes:
  - ./vw-data:/data

Backup command:

tar -czf vw-backup-$(date +%F).tar.gz vw-data/

💡 Tip: keep backups outside Docker volumes.

docs.title: Backup script
docs.text:
#!/bin/bash
BACKUP_DIR="/backups/vaultwarden"
DATA_DIR="/vaultwarden"
DATE=$(date +%F)

mkdir -p "$BACKUP_DIR"

tar -czf "$BACKUP_DIR/vw-$DATE.tar.gz" \
  "$DATA_DIR/db.sqlite3" \
  "$DATA_DIR/db.sqlite3-wal" \
  "$DATA_DIR/attachments" \
  "$DATA_DIR/rsa_key.pem" \
  "$DATA_DIR/rsa_key.pub.pem"

docs.title: Cron (daily at 3 AM)
docs.text: 0 3 * * * /usr/local/bin/vw-backup.sh

docs.title: Encrypt backup (GPG)
docs.text: gpg -c vw-2026-02-05.tar.gz

docs.title: Off-site ideas
docs.text:
• NAS snapshot
  • rsync to another server
  • rclone → Google Drive / S3 / OneDrive
  • Immutable storage (best)

2-1-1 rule

2 copies, 1 off-site, 1 encrypted

docs.title: Restore procedure
docs.text:
docker stop vaultwarden
rm -rf /vaultwarden/*
tar -xzf vw-backup-YYYY-MM-DD.tar.gz -C /vaultwarden
docker start vaultwarden

docs.title: Verification checklist
docs.text:
• Web UI loads
  • Can log in
  • Attachments open
  • Organizations intact

🚨 If you’ve never tested restore, your backup is theoretical.

docs.title: 9. Disaster Scenarios & What Saves You
docs.text: Scenario Required backup Server disk failure Full directory backup Accidental delete Recent snapshot Ransomware Offline copy Corrupted DB Multiple dated backups Forgot admin password Restore DB

docs.title: 10. What NOT to Rely On
docs.text:
❌ Bitwarden client export only

❌ VM snapshot without file awareness

❌ Cloud provider backup alone

❌ Single copy on same disk

docs.title: 11. Advanced Tips (Power Users)
docs.text:
• Enable filesystem snapshots (ZFS/Btrfs)
  • Use read-only backup user
  • Rotate backups (e.g. keep 30 days)
  • Monitor backup success (email/Telegram)
  • Version-lock Vaultwarden during restore

docs.title: 12. Minimal Checklist (Print This)
docs.text:
• db.sqlite3 backed up
  • attachments/ backed up
  • rsa_key.pem backed up
  • Off-site copy exists
  • Restore tested
