docs.text: • Zotero 中文社区

docs.title: 1. What is Zotero (and why you should care)
docs.text:
Zotero is a free, open-source reference manager. It helps you:

  • Collect academic papers, books, websites
  • Store PDFs and notes in one place
  • Automatically generate citations and bibliographies
  • Insert citations into Word / LibreOffice / Google Docs

In short:

👉 Zotero saves you from citation hell.

If you’ve ever:

  • Lost a PDF
  • Forgotten where a quote came from
  • Spent hours formatting references

Zotero exists to stop that suffering 😌

docs.title: 2. What Zotero is not
docs.text:
Let’s clear this up early:

  • ❌ Not a PDF reader replacement (it has one, but it’s basic)
  • ❌ Not a cloud drive (sync is limited unless you pay)
  • ❌ Not plagiarism detection software

Think of Zotero as your research brain + filing cabinet.

docs.title: 3. Zotero’s core components
docs.text: Zotero has three parts. You usually need all of them.

docs.title: 3.1 Zotero Desktop (the main app)
docs.text:
• Runs on macOS / Windows / Linux
  • This is where your library lives

You’ll see:

  • Left pane: Collections (folders)
  • Middle pane: Items (papers, books, etc.)
  • Right pane: Metadata, notes, tags

docs.title: 3.2 Browser Connector (VERY important)
docs.text:
This is the magic part ✨

  • Works in Chrome / Firefox / Edge / Safari
  • One click → save citation + PDF (if available)

Examples:

  • On Google Scholar → saves paper + PDF
  • On JSTOR → saves metadata + full text
  • On Amazon → saves book info

👉 Always install this.

docs.title: 3.3 Word / Google Docs Plugin
docs.text:
This lets you:

  • Insert citations while writing
  • Automatically build a bibliography
  • Change citation styles later (APA → MLA → Chicago)

You do not manually type references anymore. Ever.

docs.title: 4. Installing Zotero (quick guide)
docs.text:
1. Go to zotero.org
  2. Download:
    • Zotero Desktop
    • Browser Connector
  3. Open Zotero → Settings → check:
    • Citation plugin installed successfully

That’s it. No account required (yet).

docs.title: 5.1 Items vs Collections
docs.text:
Important concept:

  • Item = a reference (paper, book, webpage)
  • Collection = a folder (can contain the same item multiple times)

You can:

  • Put one paper in multiple collections
  • Delete a collection without deleting the item

This is tag-like organization, not file-system hell.

docs.title: 5.2 Common item types
docs.text:
Zotero supports many types:

  • Journal Article
  • Book
  • Book Chapter
  • Conference Paper
  • Thesis
  • Webpage

Choose the correct type → citation formatting works correctly.

docs.title: 6.1 Best method: Browser Connector ⭐⭐⭐
docs.text:
1. Open a paper page
  2. Click the Zotero icon in your browser
  3. Done

Zotero automatically grabs:

  • Title
  • Authors
  • Journal
  • Year
  • DOI
  • PDF (if available)

This is how you should add 90% of items.

docs.title: 6.2 Drag & drop PDFs (works, but…)
docs.text:
You can drag a PDF into Zotero.

Then:

  • Right-click → Retrieve Metadata for PDF

⚠️ Sometimes metadata is incomplete or wrong. Always double-check.

docs.title: 6.3 Manual entry (last resort)
docs.text:
Use when:

  • Old books
  • Non-academic sources
  • Bad PDFs

Click + New Item → choose type → fill fields carefully.

docs.title: 7.1 Built-in PDF reader
docs.text:
Zotero has:

  • Highlighting
  • Comments
  • Page-linked annotations

Your highlights are searchable inside Zotero 👀

docs.title: 7.2 Notes (very underrated)
docs.text:
You can create:

  • Item notes (for one reference)
  • Standalone notes (for ideas, summaries)

Pro tip:

  • Write why the paper matters, not just what it says.

docs.title: 8. Tags & search (this is where Zotero shines)
8.1 Tags
docs.text:
• Auto-tags from metadata
  • Manual tags you add

Examples:

  • method:survey
  • theory:constructivism
  • important

Tags = flexible organization without moving files.

docs.title: 8.2 Advanced search
docs.text:
You can search by:

  • Author
  • Title
  • Tag
  • Year
  • Even full-text inside PDFs

Zotero becomes a research database, not just storage.

docs.title: 9.1 Insert citations
docs.text:
In Word / Google Docs:

  1. Click Add Citation
  2. Search by author / title
  3. Select reference
  4. Done

Zotero handles:

  • In-text citations
  • Footnotes
  • Multiple citations at once

docs.title: 9.2 Bibliography (automatic)
docs.text:
At the end:

  • Click Add Bibliography

If you:

  • Add or remove citations
  • Change citation style

👉 The bibliography updates automatically.

Yes, it’s as good as it sounds.

docs.title: 10. Citation styles (APA, MLA, etc.)
docs.text:
Zotero supports:

  • APA
  • MLA
  • Chicago
  • IEEE
  • Vancouver
  • Thousands more

You can:

  • Switch styles with one click
  • Install custom styles (.csl files)

Never reformat references manually again.

docs.title: 11.1 Zotero sync
docs.text:
Zotero can sync:

  • Metadata (free, unlimited)
  • PDFs (free up to 300MB)

Create a Zotero account → log in on multiple devices.

docs.title: 11.2 Smart backup strategy (recommended)
docs.text:
Even if you sync:

  • Regularly back up your Zotero data directory
  • Or export your library as .zotero.sqlite / .rdf

Think of Zotero as critical research data.

docs.title: 12. Common beginner mistakes
docs.text:
Avoid these 👇

  • ❌ Manually typing references in Word
  • ❌ Using “Webpage” for journal articles
  • ❌ Never checking imported metadata
  • ❌ Relying on Zotero sync as your only backup
  • ❌ Storing PDFs outside Zotero without links

docs.title: 13. Zotero vs alternatives (quick take)
docs.text:
• Zotero: free, open-source, flexible ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐
  • Mendeley: owned by Elsevier, more closed
  • EndNote: powerful but expensive and heavy

For most students and researchers:

👉 Zotero is the best default choice.

docs.title: 14. How to grow after this
docs.text:
Once you’re comfortable, you can explore:

  • Better BibTeX (for LaTeX users)
  • Group libraries (team research)
  • Linked notes + Zettelkasten workflows
  • External PDF readers (Zotero still tracks metadata)

docs.title: fd
docs.text: A faster, simpler replacement for find

docs.title: 1. What is fd?
docs.text:
fd is a command-line tool for finding files and directories.

Think of it as:

find, but human-friendly

fd is designed with sane defaults, clear syntax, and excellent performance.

docs.title: 2. Why use fd?
docs.text:
Compared to find, fd:

  • ⚡ Is much faster
  • ✨ Has simple syntax
  • 🧠 Uses smart defaults
  • 🚫 Respects .gitignore
  • 🎨 Has colored output
  • 🦀 Written in Rust

docs.title: macOS (Homebrew)
docs.text:
brew install fd

On macOS, the binary is usually named fd.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
sudo apt install fd-find

On some distros, use:

fdisk --version

Then create an alias:

alias fd=fdfind

docs.title: 4.1 Find files by name
docs.text:
fd main

Finds all files and directories with main in the name.

docs.title: 4.2 Find only files
docs.text: fd -t f main

docs.title: Find only directories
docs.text: fd -t d src

docs.title: 4.3 Search in a specific directory
docs.text: fd main src/

docs.title: 5. Pattern matching (very important)
docs.text: By default, fd uses regular expressions.

docs.title: Simple substring match
docs.text:
fd test

Matches:

test.c
my_test_file.txt

docs.title: Exact match
docs.text: fd '^main$'

docs.title: File extension
docs.text: fd '\.c$'

docs.title: 6. Case sensitivity
docs.text: • Case-sensitive by default

docs.title: Case-insensitive search
docs.text: fd -i readme

docs.title: 7. Ignore rules
docs.text:
By default, fd ignores:

  • .gitignore
  • .ignore
  • .fdignore
  • Hidden files

docs.title: Include hidden files
docs.text: fd -H config

docs.title: Ignore .gitignore
docs.text: fd -I main

docs.title: Exclude a directory
docs.text: fd main -E target

docs.title: Exclude multiple paths
docs.text: fd main -E node_modules -E .git

docs.title: 9. Run commands on results (-x)
docs.text: One of the most powerful features.

docs.title: Example: delete matched files
docs.text: fd '\.tmp$' -x rm

docs.title: Format:
docs.text: fd PATTERN -x command {}

docs.title: Example: open files in editor
docs.text: fd '\.c$' -x vim

docs.title: 10. Combine fd with rg
docs.text:
Find files first, then search inside them:

fd '\.c$' | xargs rg malloc

docs.title: Search only current directory
docs.text: fd main -d 1

docs.title: 12. Show full paths
docs.text: fd main -p

docs.title: 13. fd vs find (quick comparison)
docs.text: Feature fd find Simple syntax ✅ ❌ Fast ⚡ 🐢 .gitignore aware ✅ ❌ Colored output ✅ ❌

docs.title: ❌ Using *
docs.text: fd *.c   # ❌

docs.title: ✅ Correct
docs.text: fd '\.c$'

docs.title: ❌ Expecting glob behavior
docs.text: Remember: regex, not glob.

docs.title: 15. Typical workflow examples
docs.text:
fd readme
fd '\.md$'
fd -t d src
fd test -E build
fd '\.log$' -x rm

docs.title: 16. Summary
docs.text:
fd gives you:

  • Faster file searches
  • Cleaner syntax
  • Safer defaults
  • Less typing

Once you try it, going back to find feels painful.

docs.title: 17. Recommended tool combo
docs.text:
Task Tool Jump directories zoxide Find files fd Search content ripgrep Interactive filter fzf

A modern terminal stack 🚀

docs.title: 1. What is fzf?
docs.text:
fzf is a command-line fuzzy finder.

It lets you:

  • Search files, directories, command history, git commits, etc.
  • Type partial keywords instead of exact matches
  • Interactively select items in a fast, keyboard-driven UI

Think of it as:

“Ctrl + F for your terminal, but much smarter.”

docs.title: 2. What “Fuzzy” Means
docs.text:
Traditional search:

README

fzf fuzzy search:

rdm

fzf will still match:

README.md

Because it matches characters in order, not strictly contiguous.

docs.title: macOS (recommended)
docs.text:
brew install fzf

Then enable key bindings:

$(brew --prefix)/opt/fzf/install

Choose yes for shell key bindings and completion.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
sudo apt install fzf

or

sudo pacman -S fzf

docs.title: Check installation
docs.text: fzf --version

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
ls | fzf

What happens:

  1. ls outputs filenames
  2. fzf displays them in an interactive list
  3. You type → list filters instantly
  4. Press Enter → selected item is printed

docs.title: 5. Basic fzf Interface
docs.text:
When fzf opens:

Key Action Type Fuzzy filter ↑ / ↓ Move selection Ctrl + j / k Move selection Enter Confirm Esc / Ctrl + c Exit

docs.title: 6. Useful Built-in Key Bindings (VERY IMPORTANT)
docs.text: After installation, fzf integrates deeply with your shell.

docs.title: Ctrl + T — File picker
docs.text:
vim <Ctrl+t>

Select a file → it is inserted into the command line.

docs.title: Ctrl + R — Command history search
docs.text:
<Ctrl+r>

Search your shell history interactively.

This alone makes fzf worth installing.

docs.title: Alt + C — Directory jump
docs.text:
<Alt+c>

Quickly jump to any directory.

docs.title: Open a file with vim
docs.text: vim $(fzf)

docs.title: cd into a directory
docs.text: cd $(find . -type d | fzf)

docs.title: Kill a process
docs.text: ps aux | fzf | awk '{print $2}' | xargs kill

docs.title: Git branch switch
docs.text: git branch | fzf | xargs git checkout

docs.title: 8. Preview Window (Game Changer)
docs.text: fzf can show a preview pane.

docs.title: Preview files
docs.text: fzf --preview 'cat {}'

docs.title: Preview directories
docs.text: fzf --preview 'ls {}'

docs.title: Syntax-highlight preview (if you have bat)
docs.text: fzf --preview 'bat --style=numbers --color=always {}'

docs.title: 9. Search Inside Files (ripgrep + fzf)
docs.text:
Install ripgrep:

brew install ripgrep

Search file contents:

rg --line-number "" | fzf

Advanced:

rg "" --line-number | fzf --preview 'sed -n {1}p {2}'

docs.title: Search git commits
docs.text: git log --oneline | fzf

docs.title: Search changed files
docs.text: git status --short | fzf

docs.title: 11. Environment Variables (Simple Customization)
docs.text:
Example:

export FZF_DEFAULT_OPTS="--height=40% --layout=reverse --border"

Common options:

  • --height=40% → floating window
  • --layout=reverse → prompt at bottom
  • --border → nicer UI

docs.title: 12. fzf Completion
docs.text:
After installation, fzf replaces default shell completion.

Example:

ssh <Tab>

You’ll get an interactive fzf menu.

Works with:

  • cd
  • ssh
  • kill
  • git checkout
  • many more

docs.title: 13. When Should You Use fzf?
docs.text:
Use fzf when:

  • You have too many files
  • You forget exact names
  • You want speed without mouse
  • You live in the terminal (Git, SSH, Docker, logs)

docs.title: 14. fzf vs grep vs find
docs.text:
Tool Best for grep Scriptable text search find File system queries fzf Interactive selection

fzf does not replace them — it enhances them.

docs.title: 15. Minimal Daily Workflow Example
docs.text:
vim $(fzf)
cd $(find . -type d | fzf)
git checkout $(git branch | fzf)
history | fzf

docs.title: 16. Summary
docs.text:
• fzf is a fuzzy interactive selector
  • Works with stdin / stdout
  • Integrates deeply with your shell
  • Key bindings: Ctrl-T, Ctrl-R, Alt-C
  • Becomes addictive very quickly 😄

docs.title: Ripgrep (rg)
docs.text: A fast, modern replacement for grep

docs.title: 1. What is ripgrep?
docs.text:
ripgrep (command: rg) is a search tool that lets you search text inside files.

Think of it as:

grep, but much faster and smarter

It is especially popular among developers because it:

  • Is extremely fast
  • Respects .gitignore automatically
  • Has simple, intuitive syntax

docs.title: 2. Why use ripgrep?
docs.text:
Compared to traditional grep, ripgrep:

  • ⚡ Searches very fast (written in Rust)
  • 🚫 Automatically ignores .gitignore files
  • 📁 Searches directories recursively by default
  • 🧠 Has sane defaults (no extra flags needed)
  • 🛠️ Works well with editors (VS Code, Neovim, etc.)

docs.title: macOS (Homebrew)
docs.text: brew install ripgrep

docs.title: Linux
docs.text: sudo apt install ripgrep

docs.title: Verify installation
docs.text: rg --version

docs.title: 4.1 Search for a word in the current directory
docs.text:
rg main

This:

  • Searches all files
  • Recursively
  • Skips ignored files (.gitignore, .ignore)

docs.title: 4.2 Search in a specific directory
docs.text: rg main src/

docs.title: 4.3 Search in a specific file
docs.text: rg main main.c

docs.title: 5. Understanding the output
docs.text:
Example:

src/main.c
12:int main() {

Meaning:

[file path]
[line number]:[matched line]

Matches are highlighted automatically.

docs.title: Case-sensitive (default)
docs.text: rg Hello

docs.title: Case-insensitive
docs.text: rg -i hello

docs.title: 7. Search using regular expressions
docs.text: ripgrep supports regex by default.

docs.title: Example: match foo or bar
docs.text: rg "foo|bar"

docs.title: Match numbers
docs.text:
rg "\d+"

(No -E needed!)

docs.title: By file extension
docs.text: rg main -g "*.c"

docs.title: Exclude files
docs.text: rg main -g "!*.test.js"

docs.title: 9. Search hidden files
docs.text: By default, hidden files are ignored.

docs.title: Include hidden files
docs.text: rg --hidden

docs.title: Ignore .gitignore
docs.text: rg --no-ignore

docs.title: Files that contain matches
docs.text: rg -l main

docs.title: Files that do NOT contain matches
docs.text: rg -L main

docs.title: Count matching lines per file
docs.text: rg -c main

docs.title: Count total matches
docs.text: rg -c main | awk -F: '{sum+=$2} END {print sum}'

docs.title: 12. Preview matches interactively (with fzf)
docs.text:
If you have fzf installed:

rg main | fzf

Or with preview:

rg main --line-number | fzf --preview 'bat --highlight-line {2} {1}'

docs.title: ❌ Using rg *
docs.text:
ripgrep does not need \*.

✅ Correct:

rg keyword

docs.title: ❌ Forgetting regex behavior
docs.text:
. means “any character”.

To search literal dots:

rg "\."

docs.title: 14. ripgrep vs grep (quick comparison)
docs.text: Feature rg grep Recursive by default ✅ ❌ .gitignore aware ✅ ❌ Speed ⚡ 🐢 Regex by default ✅ ❌

docs.title: 15. When should you use ripgrep?
docs.text:
Use rg when you want to:

  • Search codebases
  • Find functions, variables, strings
  • Replace grep -R
  • Work fast in the terminal

docs.title: 16. Typical workflow example
docs.text:
rg malloc
rg TODO
rg "error|fail"
rg main src/

Fast. Simple. Powerful.

docs.title: 17. Summary
docs.text:
ripgrep (rg) is:

  • Fast
  • Simple
  • Powerful
  • Developer-friendly

If you work with text or code, it’s one of the most useful CLI tools you can learn.

docs.title: Zoxide
docs.text:
A smarter cd command

  • z
  • zi

docs.title: 1. What is zoxide?
docs.text:
zoxide is a modern replacement for the cd command.

It learns which directories you use the most and lets you jump to them instantly—without typing long paths.

docs.title: Traditional cd
docs.text: cd ~/Documents/projects/my-awesome-project/src

docs.title: With zoxide
docs.text:
z my-awesome

That’s it.

docs.title: 2. Why use zoxide?
docs.text:
zoxide is useful because it:

  • 🧠 Learns automatically from your directory usage
  • ⚡ Saves keystrokes (jump with partial names)
  • 🔍 Uses frecency (frequency + recency)
  • 🐚 Works with zsh, bash, fish, nushell
  • 🛠️ Is fast and written in Rust

If you frequently cd around your system, zoxide is a huge productivity boost.

docs.title: macOS (Homebrew)
docs.text: brew install zoxide

docs.title: Linux (most distros)
docs.text:
sudo apt install zoxide

or via cargo:

cargo install zoxide

docs.title: Verify installation
docs.text: zoxide --version

docs.title: 4. Enable zoxide in your shell
docs.text: zoxide needs a small shell hook to work.

docs.title: For zsh (most common on macOS)
docs.text:
Add this to ~/.zshrc:

eval "$(zoxide init zsh)"

Then reload:

source ~/.zshrc

docs.title: For bash
docs.text:
Add to ~/.bashrc:

eval "$(zoxide init bash)"

docs.title: For fish
docs.text: zoxide init fish | source

docs.title: 5.1 Jump to a directory
docs.text:
z project

zoxide searches your directory history and jumps to the best match.

Example:

z code
z downloads
z dotfiles

docs.title: 5.2 Partial matching (very powerful)
docs.text:
z my

If you’ve visited:

~/my-project
~/my-notes

zoxide picks the one you use most often.

docs.title: 5.3 Multiple keywords
docs.text:
z work backend

Matches directories containing both words.

docs.title: 6. How does zoxide learn?
docs.text:
zoxide automatically records directories when you:

  • cd into them
  • Use z to jump

It does not scan your filesystem. It only learns from your behavior.

Over time, it becomes more accurate.

docs.title: List known directories
docs.text: zoxide query -l

docs.title: Show match score
docs.text: zoxide query my-project

docs.title: Jump using interactive selection (fzf)
docs.text:
If you have fzf installed:

zi

You get a searchable list of all known directories.

docs.title: 8. Replace cd completely (optional)
docs.text: If you want zoxide to feel native:

docs.title: zsh alias
docs.text:
alias cd="z"

Now every cd becomes smart automatically.

⚠️ Optional, but many users love it.

docs.title: ❓ Is zoxide safe?
docs.text:
Yes.

  • No background daemon
  • No network access
  • Stores a small local database

docs.title: ❓ Where is the data stored?
docs.text:
Usually in:

~/.local/share/zoxide/

docs.title: ❓ Does it slow down the shell?
docs.text: No. zoxide is extremely fast.

docs.title: 10. Typical workflow example
docs.text:
cd ~/Documents/projects/website
cd src
cd components

Later…

z website
z components

No long paths. No thinking.

docs.title: 11. zoxide vs autojump
docs.text:
Feature zoxide autojump Language Rust Python Speed ⚡ Fast Slower Matching Better Basic Maintenance Active Less

zoxide is generally considered the modern successor.

docs.title: 12. Summary
docs.text:
zoxide gives you:

  • Faster navigation
  • Less typing
  • Smarter jumps
  • Zero configuration after setup

If you use the terminal daily, zoxide is a must-have tool.
